articles.title: I Used gp-grid to Build a React Food Festival App with Advanced Data Grid Features
articles.description: I had already explored gp-grid's features and capabilities, and I wrote gp-grid: A Free, Open-Source...
articles.body_html:
I had already explored gp-grid's features and capabilities, and I wrote gp-grid: A Free, Open-Source TypeScript Data Grid for React, Vue, and Angular (No Paywalled Features)

So I wanted to see how gp-grid's features would work together in an actual React application. I wanted a project with different types of data, enough records to make the grids useful, and interactions that would put the library's features to practical use.

For that, I built STREET BITES, a fictional international street food festival website where visitors can discover dishes, explore food vendors, and browse a three-day event schedule.

The application has four pages. I used gp-grid across three data-driven pages, with features such as sorting, filtering, custom cell renderers, inline editing, row grouping, pivoting, and virtual scrolling.

In this article, I'll walk through how I built the application, the gp-grid features I implemented, and my experience using it in a real React project.

TL;DR

gp-grid is a free, open-source TypeScript data grid for React, Vue, and Angular. After using it to build STREET BITES, I found it straightforward to integrate into a React application, with advanced grid features available through one package.

  • Project: I built STREET BITES, a four-page React website for a fictional international street food festival.
  • Grid integration: gp-grid powers the Vendor Directory, Food Explorer, and Festival Schedule.
  • Features tested: Sorting, filtering, custom cell renderers, inline editing, row selection, grouping, pivoting, virtual scrolling, and live updates.
  • Developer experience: Installation and initial setup were simple, and the library fitted naturally into my React and TypeScript project.
  • Biggest strengths: Advanced features come with the Apache 2.0 package, custom renderers offer plenty of flexibility, and the core setup stays clean.

My overall experience was positive. I'd consider gp-grid for data-heavy React applications that need advanced functionality without a feature-based license fee, while teams with strict adoption requirements should evaluate its maturity and support options.

What Is gp-grid?

gp-grid is an open-source TypeScript data grid released under the Apache 2.0 license, with official integrations for React, Vue, and Angular. Its framework-agnostic core supports features such as sorting, filtering, editing, grouping, pivoting, and slot-based virtual scrolling. The project has reached version 1.0.0, and all features are available without a paid tier.

What I Built?

STREET BITES is a fictional international street food festival website built to give this gp-grid review a practical foundation. It brings together food vendors, international dishes, and festival events in one place, creating several realistic data exploration scenarios.

What Is STREET BITES?

The festival takes place from June 12 to 14, 2027, at Riverside Park in Old Harbour. Its tagline is "A world of flavor. One incredible festival." The fictional event brings together vendors from 15 countries, hundreds of dishes, and 72 activities, including cooking demonstrations, food competitions, chef talks, workshops, tastings, and live music.

Visitors can explore the vendors, discover dishes from different cuisines, and check the three-day event schedule. All festival information and records in the project are fictional.

Why I Chose a Street Food Festival

I wanted a project with different types of data and interactions that would make sense to visitors. A food festival provides plenty of opportunities to sort and filter records by cuisine, country, price, rating, dietary category, and availability.

It also creates useful scenarios for grouping vendors by location or cuisine, analyzing availability with a pivot view, and displaying event status changes. Food images, ratings, badges, and spice indicators give the grids room for custom cell rendering, too.

The Four Pages and Their Purpose

STREET BITES has four main pages, each serving a different part of the festival experience:

  • Home: Introduces the festival with featured vendors, popular dishes, statistics, highlights, and upcoming events.
  • Vendors: Lists 10,000 food vendors with information about their cuisine, country, festival zone, stall, rating, and current status.
  • Food Explorer: Presents a catalog of 5,000 dishes with prices, dietary categories, spice levels, ratings, and popularity scores.
  • Schedule: Organizes 72 events across three days, with details about times, stages, hosts, categories, and live statuses.

The Home page uses regular React components for its editorial sections and featured cards. The other three pages use gp-grid to power their interactive data exploration experiences.

You can check out the full project and explore the food yourself.

Live Demo 👀

GitHub Repository ⭐

Technology Stack and Project Setup

STREET BITES uses a React and TypeScript stack, with gp-grid handling the interactive data grids across its three main exploration pages. The rest of the interface uses familiar React components, keeping navigation, filters, featured cards, and festival sections separate from the grid implementation.

Technologies Used

Here is the stack behind the project:

  • React: Builds the website interface and reusable components.
  • TypeScript: Defines the data models for vendors, dishes, and festival events, helping keep the application code consistent.
  • Vite: Handles the development server and production build.
  • Tailwind CSS: Styles the website, including its colorful cards, responsive layouts, and festival-inspired design.
  • React Router: Handles navigation between the four routes: /, /vendors, /food, and /schedule.
  • gp-grid (@gp-grid/react): Powers the interactive data grids on the Vendors, Food Explorer, and Schedule pages.

Installing gp-grid in a React Project

Adding gp-grid to a React project takes one package installation command:

npm install @gp-grid/react

The React integration requires React 18 or higher, with TypeScript 5.0 or higher recommended. Once the package is installed, import its stylesheet once at the application root:

import "@gp-grid/react/dist/styles.css";

This loads the grid's default styling across the application. You can then customize its appearance to fit your website's design.

Integrating gp-grid into the Application

A basic gp-grid integration has three main parts: column definitions, row data, and the Grid component. The grid also needs a parent container with an explicit height because it fills the available space inside that container.

For example, a vendor grid can start with a couple of column definitions and an array of vendor records:

import { Grid, type ColumnDefinition } from "@gp-grid/react";

const columns: ColumnDefinition[] = [
  { field: "name", cellDataType: "text", headerName: "Vendor", width: 220 },
  { field: "rating", cellDataType: "number", headerName: "Rating", width: 100 },
];

<div style={{ height: "520px" }}>
  <Grid columns={columns} rowData={vendors} rowHeight={56} />
</div>

Here, columns defines which fields appear and how they are displayed, while vendors supplies the records. The rowHeight property sets the height of each data row.

In STREET BITES, regular React components handle the controls around each grid, including search fields, filters, view tabs, and dataset selectors. gp-grid handles the actual data-grid experience.

Implementing gp-grid Across the Three Main Pages

I used gp-grid on three STREET BITES pages: the Vendor Directory, Food Explorer, and Festival Schedule. Each grid handles a different type of information, so I could work with vendor records, food catalogs, and event schedules in one application.

Vendor Directory: Managing and Exploring Food Vendors

The Vendor Directory contains 10,000 fictional food vendors, with summary cards showing 10,000 total vendors, 8,242 currently serving, 1819 featured vendors, and an average rating of 4.30.

The gp-grid table displays each vendor's photo, name, city, cuisine, country, festival zone, stall number, rating, review count, number of dishes, average price, and availability status. Above it, visitors can search the directory, choose a dataset size, and filter vendors by cuisine, country, zone, status, minimum rating, or featured status.

The page also includes three views: Directory, Grouped, and Pivot, giving the vendor data different ways to be explored.

 

Food Explorer: Creating an Interactive Dish Catalog

The Food Explorer contains 5,000 fictional dishes from different countries and cuisines. Three featured dishes, Tteokbokki, Bulgogi Bao, and Elote, appear above the main catalog, giving visitors a quick look at some of the festival's popular food options.

The Full Menu grid displays dish thumbnails, names, short descriptions, prices, cuisines, countries, dietary categories, spice levels, ratings, popularity scores, and availability. Visitors can narrow the catalog using filters for cuisine, country, diet, price, spice level, and status.

This page also gives the grid a more visual role, with food thumbnails, colorful dietary badges, flame icons, and popularity indicators appearing alongside the dish information.

 

Festival Schedule: Organizing Events and Activities

The Festival Schedule brings together 72 events taking place across the festival's three days. Its overview cards show 72 total events, 60 upcoming, 3 live now, and 9 completed, with an On Now banner highlighting current activities.

The gp-grid table displays each event's time, name, category, stage, host, status, featured indicator, and festival day. Visitors can switch between Day 1 (Friday, June 12), Day 2 (Saturday, June 13), Day 3 (Sunday, June 14), and All Days. Additional filters cover event category, stage, and status.

This gives visitors a practical way to explore cooking demonstrations, competitions, workshops, chef appearances, tastings, and live performances throughout the festival.

gp-grid Features I Tested in a Real React Application

Sorting and Multi-Column Sorting

Sorting works across all three grids. Clicking a column header sorts its records, while holding Shift and clicking another header adds a secondary sort. The headers display sort arrows and numbered badges to show the sorting order. For example, I can sort vendors by cuisine and then by rating to organize vendors within each cuisine. Large datasets also use Web Worker sorting by default through the client data source's useWorker option.

 

Filtering and Search

I used two filtering layers: page-level controls above each grid and the filter popup available from individual column headers. The popup supports type-specific operators for text, numbers, and dates, along with checkbox-based value selection and grouped AND/OR conditions. Filters applied to different columns combine with AND, giving visitors more control over the records they see.

 

Custom Cell Renderers

Custom cell renderers made a big difference to the visual experience. I used them for vendor photos, city and cuisine details, dish thumbnails, dietary badges, star ratings, price labels, spice flames, popularity bars, host avatars, and status pills. Pairing a renderer with a valueFormatter also helps keep filtering and copied values consistent with what users see.

 

Inline Editing

I added an Organizer mode toggle to enable editing across the vendor, dish, and event grids. Columns become editable when configured with editable: true. Users can start editing with a double-click, Enter, F2, or by typing. Enter commits a change, Tab commits and moves to the next cell, and Escape cancels it. A fill handle also copies values across a dragged range. Changes update the application state, so related page content stays in sync.

 

Row Selection and Data Comparison

The Vendors and Food Explorer pages include selection checkboxes, allowing visitors to select up to four records. The selected vendors or dishes then appear in a comparison panel, where their details are displayed side by side. I connected grid selection to React state, so the panel updates as soon as the selection changes. gp-grid also supports cell and range selection through mouse and keyboard interactions.

 

Row Grouping and Aggregation

The Vendors page includes a Grouped view that organizes records into expandable groups by cuisine, country, or festival zone. The Schedule page also supports grouping events by day, category, or stage. gp-grid can display aggregates and group totals, calculated locally or loaded from a server. This makes large collections easier to navigate while keeping related records together.

 

Pivoting

The Pivot view gives festival organizers a quick overview of vendor availability. I configured cuisines as rows, availability statuses as columns, and vendor counts as values. This creates a useful summary of how many vendors in each cuisine are Open, Busy, Sold Out, or Closed. The view uses gp-grid's pivot functionality, so the result is an actual grid pivot, not a manually assembled table.

 

Virtual Scrolling

gp-grid uses reusable DOM slots for virtual scrolling. As visitors move through a dataset, the grid recycles these slots and renders the visible rows with a small overscan buffer. The Vendors and Food Explorer pages include dataset selectors, allowing visitors to switch between different list sizes. This provides a practical way to explore how the grids handle longer catalogs without rendering every record at once.

 

Live Data Updates

The Schedule page includes a Live updates toggle that simulates changes during the festival. Events move between Upcoming, Live, and Completed, while the On Now banner and summary counts update accordingly. Vendor availability also changes between Open, Busy, Sold Out, and Closed. These updates modify the underlying records and application state, keeping the grid and related interface elements consistent.

 

Column Resizing, Reordering, and Pinning

Visitors can customize the grid layout by dragging column headers to reorder them, resizing columns from their edges, and using the pin icon to keep important columns on the left or right. The pin control cycles between left, right, and unpinned states. These interactions are useful when a grid contains many fields and visitors want to keep key information visible while exploring other columns.

 

Keyboard Navigation and Editing Experience

Keyboard navigation supports arrow keys, Shift+Arrow, Tab, Enter, Home/End, and Ctrl+Home/End. Users can start editing with Enter or F2, cancel with Escape, and copy or paste using Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V. For example, an organizer can move to a vendor's stall number, edit it, and commit the change without using the mouse. The grid also provides ARIA grid roles and keyboard support, although full accessibility compliance should not be assumed.

 

Dark Mode

I also implemented dark mode for the gp-grid tables in STREET BITES. The grid's appearance changes to a dark theme, adapting elements such as cell backgrounds, text, borders, and column headers while keeping the data easy to read. This gives users a more comfortable way to view the tables in low-light environments and shows how the grid can be styled to fit different interface themes.

 

Responsive Tables

I also checked how the gp-grid tables behave on smaller screens. The tables remain usable on mobile devices and narrower viewports, allowing visitors to browse the data without the layout becoming difficult to navigate.

This is important for STREET BITES because visitors may want to check vendors, explore dishes, or view the festival schedule from their phones. The grid keeps the data accessible across different screen sizes.

 

Performance and Development Experience

gp-grid uses slot-based virtual scrolling, recycling DOM slots as users move through a dataset and rendering visible rows with a small overscan buffer. In STREET BITES, the Vendors and Food Explorer pages include dataset selectors, with 10,000 vendors and 5,000 dishes shown in the current project.

For a separate performance reference, gp-grid's published benchmark tested one million rows in Chrome using @gp-grid/react 0.19.0. It reported an average of 56.2 FPS while scrolling, zero dropped frames, approximately 255 MB of heap memory after loading, and 652 ms for ascending sorting. These are gp-grid's benchmark results, not measurements from STREET BITES. The project provides a pnpm bench command for reproducing its tests.

Integration with React and TypeScript

The integration felt smooth throughout development. Installing the package, defining columns, connecting data, adding custom renderers, and wiring interactions to React state were all straightforward. The built-in TypeScript types also meant I could work with typed columns and records without installing separate @types packages.

I also liked that the same column model carries across the React, Vue, and Angular integrations. Developers working with more than one of these frameworks can transfer much of their grid configuration knowledge.

What Worked Well

Having sorting, filtering, editing, selection, grouping, pivoting, and virtualization available in one open-source package made the implementation easier to organize. Custom renderers were another strong point: they helped the grids match STREET BITES' visual identity, with food thumbnails, vendor photos, ratings, and colorful badges.

The package also has zero external dependencies, and gp-grid provides feature guides and an official agent skill for AI coding assistants.

Challenges and Limitations

There are a few things worth considering:

  • Library maturity: gp-grid is a young project at version 1.0.0, with a smaller community and fewer third-party tutorials than established alternatives.
  • Accessibility: it supports ARIA grid roles and keyboard navigation, but full accessibility qualification is still planned, so teams with strict requirements should test with assistive technology.
  • Implementation detail: narrow column widths can truncate headers, so allow enough space for longer labels.

Practical Tips Before You Start

  • Give the grid container an explicit height.
  • Import the stylesheet once at the application root.
  • Pair cellRenderer with valueFormatter when displayed values need consistent formatting.
  • Use a stable getRowId for live data, and consider server-side data for very large datasets.

Who Should Use gp-grid?

gp-grid is worth considering if you're building a React, Vue, or Angular application that needs advanced data-grid features without a paid feature tier. It can suit admin interfaces, analytics tools, inventory systems, and applications that handle large tabular datasets.

It's also a good option for developers who want TypeScript support, custom cell rendering, editing, grouping, pivoting, and virtual scrolling in one package. Teams evaluating it for production should test it with their own data and requirements, especially if they need a mature ecosystem or extensive accessibility validation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is gp-grid suitable for production React applications?
It can be, with sensible evaluation. gp-grid is Apache 2.0, TypeScript-native, and offers a React integration alongside Vue and Angular support. It covered the grid requirements in STREET BITES, but it's a young project at version 1.0.0. Test it with your own data and pin the version you adopt.

Does gp-grid support sorting, filtering, and inline editing?
Yes. All three are built in. In STREET BITES, column headers support sorting and Shift+click multi-column sorting. Filters combine page-level controls with column filter popups, while Organizer mode enables inline editing through double-click, Enter, or F2.

Can a React data grid handle one million rows?
Yes, with virtualization. gp-grid uses slot-based virtual scrolling to render visible rows. In its published one-million-row benchmark, it averaged 56.2 FPS with zero dropped frames and used approximately 255 MB of memory after loading. These are the project's benchmark results, not measurements from STREET BITES. For datasets of 10 million rows or more, the performance guide recommends server-side data.

Does gp-grid support row grouping and pivoting?
Yes. Both are included features. Row grouping organizes records into expandable groups with aggregates and totals. Pivoting turns data dimensions into columns to create summary views. In STREET BITES, I used a pivot view to display vendor counts by cuisine and availability status.

Is gp-grid free and open source?
Yes. gp-grid is released under the Apache 2.0 license, which permits commercial use, modification, and distribution with the required notices. Its features are included without an Enterprise tier or feature-based paywalls. You can also support the project through its optional donations.

Final Thoughts

Building STREET BITES gave me a practical way to explore gp-grid across vendor records, food catalogs, and festival schedules. I could use its sorting, filtering, editing, grouping, pivoting, and virtualization capabilities in scenarios that made sense for the application.

I came away with a positive impression of its React integration and the range of features available under an open-source license. Its young ecosystem is worth considering before adopting it for a large production system, but gp-grid is a promising option for developers who need a capable data grid without feature-based licensing restrictions.

If you're evaluating a React data grid for your next project, I'd recommend trying gp-grid with a dataset and workflow similar to your own.

articles.title: Django 6.1's FETCH_PEERS against my own select_related
articles.description: Django 6.1 added fetch modes. With FETCH_PEERS, when you touch a foreign key on one object from a...
articles.body_html:
Django 6.1 added fetch modes. With FETCH_PEERS, when you touch a foreign key on one object from a queryset, Django loads that relation for every object the queryset returned, in one query. The classic N+1 loop becomes 2 queries without you writing select_related.

My football quiz site, ExtraTime, has 621 select_related calls and 103 prefetch_related calls in its Django API, outside the tests. I wanted to know how much of that work the new mode would have done for me.

How I measured it

The API has 6,635 tests, and a lot of them call the real endpoints through Django's test client. I installed Django 6.1.3 in a copy of the project, added a middleware that counts the SQL queries behind each request, and ran the whole suite six times:

  • the code as written
  • with every select_related call turned into a no-op
  • the same, with FETCH_PEERS on everywhere
  • with both select_related and prefetch_related turned off
  • the same, with FETCH_PEERS on
  • the code as written, with FETCH_PEERS added on top

Turning a method into a no-op was a small patch on QuerySet. One exception: a Prefetch with to_attr stayed, because the code reads that attribute and would break without it. There's no setting for a global fetch mode. You set it per queryset with .fetch_mode() or on a model's manager. For the experiment I changed the internal default that every new queryset starts with, which isn't a public API.

To compare like with like, I kept only the routes the tests called the same number of times in every run: 467 routes and 3,963 requests.

The totals

  • As written: 59,198 queries
  • Without select_related: 76,144
  • Without select_related, with FETCH_PEERS: 64,416

So taking out my select_related calls added 16,946 queries, and FETCH_PEERS won back 11,728 of them, about 69%. That's a lot for something you switch on rather than write.

With both kinds of hand tuning removed, it was 74,955 queries, and 62,887 with FETCH_PEERS.

Route by route, it never fully caught up

The total hides how it gets there. select_related made a difference on 179 routes. On none of them did FETCH_PEERS get back to the hand-tuned count. It did better on 5, partly closed the gap on 59, and made no difference at all on 115.

The biggest win was the endpoint that starts a Read the Room run: 2,245 queries over 153 requests as written, 8,018 without select_related, and 2,725 with FETCH_PEERS. That's the case it's made for, a list of objects that all touch the same relations. It still lands about 3 queries per request above the hand-tuned version, because each relation costs one extra query instead of being part of a join.

The 115 routes where it did nothing come down to two things, which I checked separately on Django's own Permission model, 16 rows:

  • One object has no peers. Loading a single permission and reading its content type takes 2 queries with or without FETCH_PEERS, and 1 with select_related. A lot of my endpoints load one game session and then walk its foreign keys. FETCH_PEERS can't help there.
  • .iterator() switches it off in practice. Looping over the list and reading each content type takes 17 queries normally and 2 with FETCH_PEERS. The same loop over .iterator() takes 17 either way. The peers are the objects already loaded, and an iterator hasn't loaded the others yet when the first one asks.

The second one showed up in a place I didn't expect. The admin's "add group" page went from 14 queries to 1,198 without select_related, and FETCH_PEERS didn't change it at all. Form choice fields iterate over their queryset with .iterator().

The prefetch that cost more than it saved

I expected that removing prefetch_related could only add queries. On 34 routes it removed them, 2,762 in total, almost all on the multiplayer game rooms.

Inviting a player to a room took 668 queries over 45 requests as written, and 162 without the prefetches. The SQL showed why. The room viewset's queryset prefetches the config table of every game type, 8 of them, so that the lobby list, which mixes game types, doesn't query per room. But the same queryset is used to look up a single room for actions like invite, leave and ready. Each of those requests paid 8 queries for config tables it never read.

It's easy to miss in the code, because the prefetch lives in a shared helper. It only stood out once each request's queries were counted.

Turning it on over code that's already tuned

With FETCH_PEERS on top of the code as written, the suite had exactly the same failures as without it, and the query count dropped by 412, under 1%. 22 routes got cheaper and 6 got slightly more expensive, by between 1 and 5 queries over all their requests. I didn't track down why those 6 went up.

The tests noticed

Without select_related, 76 tests failed against 7 as written. With FETCH_PEERS, 50 did. Many of the extra failures weren't wrong answers. They were tests that pin a query count, and this codebase has a lot of them: 92 uses of assertNumQueries and 286 of CaptureQueriesContext. That's what makes hand tuning hold up over time. Without those tests, a select_related quietly stops covering what the view reads after the next change.

Two things about upgrading to 6.1 itself

Two things came up that have nothing to do with fetch modes. django-celery-beat still declares it doesn't support Django 6.1, so I had to force the install. And five tests broke for real. Querysets combined with .union() now apply the model's default ordering, and three places in the code union values_list() queries on models with Meta.ordering. Postgres rejects the result with "ORDER BY term does not match any column in the result set". An .order_by() on each part fixes it.

What I got wrong

I started on my Mac with the test runner's --parallel. Forked workers crashed twice, once inside macOS's proxy lookup and once inside the Postgres client library, and a third run died when a failing test's result couldn't be sent back to the main process. I moved the runs into a Linux container, the way the project's CI does it, and they went through in about four minutes each.

I also thought "turning it on" would be a setting. It isn't, and patching an internal default is fine for an experiment but not something I'd ship.

And I lost raw data. After the main runs, I reran the game room tests in two of the modes to capture their SQL, and the script cleared each mode's output folder first. The totals and per-route numbers above were already computed and saved by then, but the raw per-request logs for those two runs are gone.

Caveats

Test data is small. Most tests create a handful of rows, so an N+1 costs a few queries here and far more in production. That cuts both ways. FETCH_PEERS keeps a loop at 2 queries however many rows there are, so in production it would win back more of the gap than 69%. But it still can't help a single object or an .iterator().

The patch also turned off select_related inside third-party packages like the admin, not only in my code. Only requests through the test client were counted, so Celery tasks and websockets aren't in these numbers. And this is one codebase.

What I'd take from it

  • FETCH_PEERS on top of tuned code is cheap and broke nothing here. It's a reasonable safety net for the loops nobody has looked at yet.
  • It doesn't replace select_related for views that load one object and follow its foreign keys. Keep those.
  • If a loop uses .iterator(), FETCH_PEERS won't help it.
  • Count queries per request in your tests. That's what found 8 wasted queries on every room action, which no fetch mode would have fixed.

articles.title: Node.js 26's Map.getOrInsertComputed is slower than the get-and-set it replaces
articles.description: I benchmarked Node 26.13's new Map.prototype.getOrInsertComputed: 13-18% slower than plain get-then-set on a cold map, about 40% slower on a warm one, but it collapses three concurrent async fetches for the same key into one call, and caches a rejected promise forever.
articles.body_html:
Node 26 shipped V8 14.6, and with it two new methods that have been asked for for years: Map.prototype.getOrInsert() and Map.prototype.getOrInsertComputed(). Both are meant to replace the same five-line idiom everyone has copy-pasted into a cache or a memo table at some point: look up a key, and if it isn't there, compute a default, store it, and return it.

I expected the built-in version to be at least as fast as the hand-written one, since it collapses two separate Map operations into one. It is not. On a warm cache it is about 40% slower than the code it replaces.

That was the first surprise. The second is more useful: the same method quietly gives you cache-stampede protection for async work, for free, with no extra code. The third is that if the computation fails, it keeps the failure cached forever, with no obvious way to know that from the method's name alone.

What's actually new

getOrInsertComputed(key, callbackfn) checks whether key is present. If it is, it returns the existing value and never touches callbackfn. If it isn't, it calls callbackfn(key), stores the return value under key, and returns it. getOrInsert(key, value) does the same thing but takes a plain value instead of a callback. Both exist on WeakMap too.

I ran this on Node 26.13.0 ("Lithium", released 28 October 2026), which bundles V8 14.6.202.34:

$ node --version
v26.13.0
$ node -e "console.log(process.versions.v8)"
14.6.202.34-node.40

The plain pattern it replaces looks like this:

let v = map.get(key);
if (v === undefined) {
  v = compute(key);
  map.set(key, v);
}

The new one:

const v = map.getOrInsertComputed(key, compute);

The benchmark, and the number that surprised me

I timed both patterns under two workloads: a cold map where every one of 5,000,000 keys is new (the worst case, all misses), and a warm map where the same 1,000 keys get hit 5,000,000 times (the common case for an actual cache). Five to nine repetitions each, timestamps taken with process.hrtime.bigint(), reporting the fastest and the median run.

Workload get-then-set (median) getOrInsertComputed (median) Slower by
Cold, 5M unique keys 1678ms 1978ms ~18%
Warm, 5M calls over 1,000 keys 29.7ms 41.6ms ~40%

I didn't believe the warm number at first, so I reran it with the two patterns alternating order across nine repetitions, to cancel out any CPU frequency or cache-warming drift, and added a third variant: a hand-written JavaScript function that does exactly what the native method does, called the same way (as an indirect function reference, not inlined in the loop):

function myGetOrInsertComputed(map, key, cb) {
  let v = map.get(key);
  if (v === undefined) { v = cb(key); map.set(key, v); }
  return v;
}

A1 inline get+set           : min=1645.5ms  median=1772.3ms
B1 native getOrInsertComputed: min=1890.8ms  median=1952.5ms
C1 hand-rolled JS equivalent : min=1452.6ms  median=1772.4ms
B2 native getOrInsertComputed: min=1716.6ms  median=1791.7ms
A2 inline get+set           : min=1493.2ms  median=1633.7ms
C2 hand-rolled JS equivalent : min=1556.3ms  median=1640.0ms

The native method was the slowest of the three in both orderings. A plain JavaScript function wrapping get/set and taking the same callback argument was never slower than, and sometimes faster than, the engine's own built-in. V8's JIT has had years to optimise Map.prototype.get and Map.prototype.set as monomorphic, inlineable calls. getOrInsertComputed is new, and on this build it isn't getting the same treatment yet. I have no way to confirm the exact reason from outside the engine, but the pattern across six runs and three independent implementations was consistent enough that I'm confident it isn't noise.

It does buy you something real: deduplicating concurrent work

The place getOrInsertComputed earns its keep isn't raw speed, it's async correctness. If you memoise a promise instead of a resolved value, calling it from several places for the same key before the first call resolves no longer triggers duplicate work, because the method inserts synchronously, before the promise settles:

const cache = new Map();
let fetchCalls = 0;
function fetchData(key) {
  fetchCalls++;
  return new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve(`data-for-${key}`), 30));
}
async function get(key) {
  return cache.getOrInsertComputed(key, fetchData);
}

const results = await Promise.all([get('x'), get('x'), get('x'), get('y')]);
console.log(results, fetchCalls);

[ 'data-for-x', 'data-for-x', 'data-for-x', 'data-for-y' ] 2

Three concurrent calls for x and one for y produced exactly two calls to fetchData, not four. That's the manual "in-flight promise map plus a .finally() cleanup" pattern that a lot of server code hand-rolls to avoid a cache-stampede, now free with a correct, built-in single line. This is a genuine win and the strongest reason to reach for the method at all.

But a failure gets cached forever

The same property that makes deduplication work — the engine commits the promise to the map as soon as the callback returns it, without waiting to see whether it resolves or rejects — means a rejected promise sits in the cache exactly like a resolved one would, and nothing evicts it:

let attempts = 0;
function flaky(key) {
  attempts++;
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    setTimeout(() => {
      if (attempts === 1) reject(new Error(`transient failure #${attempts}`));
      else resolve(`ok on attempt ${attempts}`);
    }, 10);
  });
}
async function tryGet(key) {
  try { return `OK: ${await cache.getOrInsertComputed(key, flaky)}`; }
  catch (e) { return `ERROR: ${e.message}`; }
}

call 1: ERROR: transient failure #1
call 2: ERROR: transient failure #1
call 3: ERROR: transient failure #1
total attempts actually made: 1

flaky() would have succeeded on attempt two. It never got the chance, because the first, failed attempt was already permanently cached under that key. Every later caller gets the same stale rejection, forever, until something deletes the key explicitly. If you reach for getOrInsertComputed to deduplicate network calls, you need a .catch() that calls cache.delete(key) on the failure path yourself; the method gives you none of that for free, and nothing in its name suggests you'd need it.

It isn't transactional either

I assumed the insert step was atomic with respect to the callback: whatever the callback does to the map, the final write should reflect that. It doesn't. The method remembers that the key was absent when it started, runs the callback, and then writes the callback's return value regardless of what happened to that key in between:

const m = new Map();
const result = m.getOrInsertComputed('k', () => {
  m.set('k', 'set-during-callback');
  return 'returned-from-callback';
});
console.log(result, m.get('k'));
// returned-from-callback returned-from-callback

Whatever the callback wrote to 'k' mid-flight is silently discarded and replaced by the callback's own return value. The same thing happens if the callback deletes the key instead of setting it: the delete is undone, and the key comes back holding the callback's return value. If your compute function has any side effect on the same map under the same key — which sounds like an edge case until you consider a callback that recurses, or one shared between two related caches — this is where it bites.

The lazy default is the whole point, and the eager one is a trap

MDN is explicit that getOrInsert() evaluates its second argument eagerly, every call, hit or miss, because that argument is just a normal JavaScript expression evaluated before the method runs — that's not a quirk of the method, it's how function calls work. getOrInsertComputed() only calls its callback on a miss. The two method names are one word apart, which makes it easy to use the cheap-looking one with an expensive default by mistake. I measured the cost of making exactly that mistake, over 200,000 calls against a 100-key warm cache (so the vast majority are hits):

getOrInsert(key, expensiveDefault())        : 531.1ms, 516.5ms, 504.2ms
getOrInsertComputed(key, expensiveDefault)  : 2.8ms, 1.6ms, 1.9ms

About 270 times slower, for a cache that is already warm and should be doing almost no work. This confirms the exact warning in MDN's own docs, and it's the kind of mistake that won't show up until the default stops being a one-liner.

What it refuses

Passing something that isn't a function as the callback throws, but the message blames the wrong thing:

> m.getOrInsertComputed('k', 'not-a-function')
TypeError: Map.prototype.getOrInsertComputed is not a function

The method itself is a function — I checked typeof m.getOrInsertComputed first, it's "function". The actual problem is the second argument, but the error reads as if the method lookup failed, which is the one place I'd expect a newcomer to go looking in the wrong file.

WeakMap's versions correctly refuse primitive keys, same as every other WeakMap method:

> new WeakMap().getOrInsert('a-string-key', 1)
TypeError: Invalid value used as weak map key

That one's unsurprising, but worth confirming it wasn't quietly relaxed for the new methods. It wasn't. And if the callback throws, the map is left exactly as it was — no half-written entry, no leftover key — which is the one place everything behaved exactly as I'd have guessed.

What I got wrong on the way

My working assumption going in was that the built-in would win on speed, since it does the lookup once internally instead of twice at the JavaScript level. I was confident enough in that assumption that my first benchmark run only tested the two patterns in one fixed order — old pattern, then new pattern — and when the new one came back slower, I didn't trust it; I assumed I'd built an unfair test, maybe because sequential integer keys from 0 upward make the two Maps grow and rehash at different points depending on which ran first. That's why the final numbers above come from a run with the order alternated nine times, plus a third, hand-rolled control implementation that rules out "the built-in is just unlucky with warm caches" as an explanation. The slowdown held up in both directions and against a plain JS equivalent, so I stopped assuming the theory was obviously true and reported what I actually measured instead.

Run it yourself

This needs Node 26 or later. If your system Node is older, the official binary needs no build step:

curl -s -o node26.tar.xz "https://nodejs.org/dist/v26.13.0/node-v26.13.0-linux-x64.tar.xz"
tar -xf node26.tar.xz
NODE=./node-v26.13.0-linux-x64/bin/node
$NODE --version

The warm/cold benchmark, trimmed to the essentials:

const N = 5_000_000, KEYS = 1000;
function compute(k) { return k * 2; }

function timeIt(fn) {
  const start = process.hrtime.bigint();
  fn();
  return Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - start) / 1e6;
}

const oldWarm = () => {
  const m = new Map();
  for (let i = 0; i < KEYS; i++) m.set(i, compute(i));
  for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    const k = i % KEYS;
    let v = m.get(k);
    if (v === undefined) { v = compute(k); m.set(k, v); }
  }
};
const newWarm = () => {
  const m = new Map();
  for (let i = 0; i < KEYS; i++) m.set(i, compute(i));
  for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) m.getOrInsertComputed(i % KEYS, compute);
};

console.log('old:', timeIt(oldWarm), 'ms');
console.log('new:', timeIt(newWarm), 'ms');

$NODE bench.mjs

Every command and snippet above ran on the same machine the numbers came from, including the download.

What to do with this

The one place I'd actually swap in getOrInsertComputed today is the in-flight promise map people already hand-roll around a shared fetch or a shared database lookup. That code usually has its own bugs — a missing .finally(), a key that never gets cleaned up — and this replaces it with something shorter and more obviously correct for the success path. It won't be more obviously correct for the failure path, though. I'd still add .catch(() => cache.delete(key)) around it myself, because this method's name gives you no hint that a single rejection sits there forever otherwise.

I would not swap it in anywhere I cared about raw throughput. A hot cache lookup that currently reads map.get(key) ?? compute-and-set is doing less work than getOrInsertComputed does on this V8 build, not more, and the benchmark above says so plainly. Leave it alone.

And if a teammate reaches for getOrInsert with anything other than a hardcoded constant as the second argument, that's worth a second look in review. The name reads as the lazy, safe default. It isn't; getOrInsertComputed is the one that's lazy, and the two are close enough in spelling that autocomplete will happily suggest the wrong one at 2am.

articles.title: I can build the product with AI. Getting the first users is harder.
articles.description: What building Brainy and MoneyBrain taught me about finding early users beyond my LinkedIn network, and what I want to try next.
articles.body_html:
With Brainy and MoneyBrain, getting the first users and growing monthly recurring revenue has been harder than building the software.

At the beginning, I used my circles on LinkedIn. It gave me somewhere to start talking about the products. Expanding beyond that network has been difficult, especially without a large budget.

That is where I want to pick up from my previous post about building products with AI. In that post, I described how I move from a brainstorm to requirements, GitHub issues, implementation, and a reviewed pull request. I can give the implementation work a scope and check the result against it.

Finding users leaves me with questions I am still working through: where to reach people who need the product, and why they would try it, return, and eventually pay.

My network gave me a place to start

Talking about Brainy and MoneyBrain on LinkedIn was a reasonable first step. I already had people I could reach there, rather than starting with an empty account and hoping someone would find a product announcement.

But a professional network is a particular audience. Someone can be interested in how I build software without needing either product. A post about my AI workflow and a post explaining why someone should use an application ask for different kinds of attention.

More visibility for me would be useful, but I also need to understand which people have the problem the product addresses. Otherwise, I could spend more time promoting it and still learn very little about demand.

A screenshot of a SaaS advice post brought this back into focus. It covered familiar recommendations: promote the product, talk to users, keep the first version small, use it yourself, and pay attention to people who leave.

Reading those points alongside my experience, I kept returning to the difficulty of reaching the next group of people without a large budget.

The post puts most of the work after launch into marketing. I would not assign a fixed percentage to it, but I agree with the underlying reminder: launching leaves a substantial amount of work ahead. For my current goal of finding users, time spent explaining the product and following up with people deserves a place in the schedule alongside implementation. Another completed issue does not tell me whether anyone new understood the offer.

Reaching outside my LinkedIn circles

The encouragement to promote the product openly is useful. Staying entirely within my familiar LinkedIn circles would leave the same audience boundary in place. I need to be willing to explain what I have built somewhere people do not already know me, and to hear that it may not be relevant to them.

I could make a long list of places to post. Each one would take time to understand, participate in, and follow up on. I would also have to decide what to say there, because a product announcement that makes sense to my LinkedIn contacts may mean very little to a stranger.

For Brainy and MoneyBrain, I would rather make the next attempt narrow enough to learn from. Pick one product, one specific problem, and one place where people already discuss that problem. Then explain or demonstrate the part of the product that addresses it.

I also need to make that choice separately for each product. The fact that I built both does not mean the same people need both, or that the same explanation will persuade them. Putting their names into one announcement is convenient for me; a potential user needs a reason to care about the particular application in front of them.

I could examine the result: did people recognize the problem, ask how the product handles their situation, or try it?

If the only response is interest in the technology behind it, that would tell me something too. I might have reached other builders, or explained the implementation more clearly than the reason to use the product.

I feel the budget constraint, but I do not want to turn that into a conclusion that growth requires a large advertising spend. I have not established that. Before spending more, I want a clearer idea of whom I am trying to reach and what I can show them.

A useful next asset could be a short walkthrough of one task, using demonstration data and showing the result. I could use it in a relevant conversation, give the landing page something concrete to show, and learn which part needs more explanation. A tutorial answering a question prospective users already ask could also become something they can find or share later. These would give me more to work with than repeatedly announcing that the product exists.

A community, a search-focused article, or a collaboration needs to earn the time I put into it. A channel with no advertising bill still costs time. Participating well in a community means reading the discussions, respecting its rules, and contributing something useful before expecting attention for my application.

The alternative is often something people already do

Before writing that walkthrough, I need to understand what the person would replace. They might already have a tool, a document, or a routine that handles the task adequately. Moving to my product could mean learning another interface and spending time setting it up before they see a benefit.

My own move from Notion to Brainy is a useful example of an existing workflow being involved. It gives me a case to examine, but another person's reasons to change could be different. I need to ask which part of their current approach is frustrating enough to justify the effort of switching.

That should shape the product description. Explaining the task someone can complete gives them a way to judge the offer. Describing my AI-assisted development process tells them how I made it. I enjoy talking about that process, and it belongs in the previous post, but it may have little bearing on a person's decision to use Brainy or MoneyBrain.

Even the comparison with competitors needs this context. A competing subscription price tells me one thing about the market; a person's current workaround tells me what I would have to improve. If their approach is already good enough, I need to understand that answer instead of assuming another feature will persuade them.

The first visit needs somewhere useful to go

Someone outside my network needs to understand the product without knowing my background. That makes the advice about the landing page and sign-up process more relevant.

A useful check would be to ask someone unfamiliar with the project to look at the page and explain what they think it does. Then ask them to attempt its main task. I would want to see where they hesitate before adding another feature to the backlog.

That is how I read the advice to make a landing page clean, fast, and convincing. Keep the page focused, check how it loads on a phone, and show a concrete use of the product. A polished layout still needs to help that unfamiliar visitor decide whether to try it.

Google login might remove a step for some people. It cannot explain an unclear product promise, and I would not treat it as an automatic requirement for every audience. The question I want to investigate is where a prospective user gets stuck between understanding the offer and experiencing something useful.

Using my own product regularly gives me a way to notice friction in ordinary tasks. In my earlier post about moving to European digital services, I described replacing Notion with Brainy. That is a useful starting point for testing a real workflow. But I know the product's intended behavior and can navigate around something that another person would find confusing. My familiarity is a reason to get an outside view, especially when I am asking that person to trust a new product.

Keeping the minimum viable product small belongs in this discussion too. I want enough functionality to let someone complete the task that brought them there. Adding features before understanding that task could make both the explanation and the first visit more complicated.

The screenshot names MoSCoW as a way to keep that scope under control: Must Have, Should Have, Could Have, and Won't Have this time. The Agile Business Consortium explains those priorities. For a first release, I would ask whether leaving a feature out prevents the intended user from completing the core task. If it does not, I need a good reason to put it ahead of learning from users.

For the first users, I would also consider helping them through that task personally. Paul Graham's essay on doing things that don't scale argues for recruiting early users manually and paying close attention to their experience. I can see a practical application here: offer a short walkthrough, watch where the person needs help, and use that observation to improve the next attempt.

If I have to explain the same step to everyone, that gives me something specific to investigate in the interface or instructions. If each person wants a completely different outcome, I need to revisit the audience and scope. Automating the welcome messages before understanding those differences could leave me sending more people through a confusing experience.

Trust is part of the first useful experience

There is another reason someone might hesitate even after understanding the product: they have to decide whether to put their information into it. A demonstration with sample data can reduce the effort needed to evaluate the workflow, but using the application for real asks for more trust.

For any task involving personal or financial information, I would want the product to explain what it stores, what happens to that information, and how a person can leave. Those explanations need to match the actual implementation. I cannot make a privacy or security promise simply because it would look reassuring on the landing page.

Support belongs in that decision too. A person should be able to find a way to report a problem and understand what help they can reasonably expect. As an independent builder, I need to be honest about that commitment. Offering personal onboarding is useful only if I leave enough time to follow through.

This is part of what makes a small MVP a serious product decision. I can defer optional features while still needing a dependable core workflow. If the application loses the work someone just entered, a smaller backlog does not make their experience acceptable. The scope has to include the behavior people rely on, and I need to check it before asking them to move a real task into the application.

Growing MRR asks more than whether someone signed up

The screenshot recommends charging from day one instead of offering free trials. There is a useful question behind that advice: will someone pay for the outcome? A payment is more direct evidence of willingness to pay than an encouraging comment on LinkedIn.

I would still make the trial decision around the product. If someone needs to use it with their own information or across several days to judge the benefit, a trial could help them decide. If the value can be demonstrated clearly before purchase, charging immediately may make sense. I would not dismiss every free user as unserious; their experience can reveal a problem that also affects paying users.

Monthly recurring revenue is an objective I care about. To make progress toward it, I need to understand what would justify an ongoing payment from the people I am trying to reach. Choosing a price or removing a free trial does not answer that question on its own.

The advice to price based on value is more useful to me than copying another application's subscription page. I would want to ask about the task a person is doing now: how they handle it, what is frustrating, and what a useful improvement would look like. Time saved, a recurring task made easier, or a mistake avoided could give the discussion a concrete basis. Those are possibilities to investigate, not benefits I can assign a monetary value to without talking to people.

Those conversations could happen through a DM, an email, or a short call, depending on what the person prefers. A focused question about what they tried to do would give me more to work with than asking whether they like the product. I would also want to hear from someone who created an account and then stopped, rather than only from people willing to praise it.

This is where retention belongs alongside the work of finding new users. If people try the product and do not return, reaching a larger audience leaves that question unresolved. I would want to understand repeated use before scaling the same acquisition attempt. For a recurring subscription, whether people keep finding a reason to use the product matters to the revenue goal too.

If a person leaves, an optional conversation could help explain what happened. I would make unsubscribing or cancelling straightforward, and respect a person who does not want to explain. An email opt-out might mean they want fewer messages; a product cancellation asks a different question. Either can be feedback, but neither gives me a reason to argue with their decision.

I also need to understand the expected frequency of the task. Someone may get value from a product every week or at a particular point in the month. Daily activity would be a poor way to judge that experience if daily use was never the goal. I would look for people returning when the need occurs and completing the task they came for.

Feedback from those conversations needs a decision attached to it. A request for another feature might reveal a missing step in the core workflow, or it might describe a different product. I would record what the person was trying to accomplish before putting the request into the backlog. That gives me a way to compare it with other needs instead of letting the most recent message determine the next epic.

I need to know where the attempt stops working

Once I start trying channels outside LinkedIn, a total sign-up count will leave too much unexplained. I want enough visibility to distinguish a message that people never saw from a product they tried and then abandoned.

A simple record could follow the path from first contact to continued use:

Step What I would try to learn
Someone encounters the product Which conversation, post, article, or recommendation brought them there?
They visit the page Can they understand the problem it addresses and the next action?
They create an account Where do they hesitate or leave during registration?
They complete the main task Do they get the outcome that made them try it?
They return when needed Does the product fit an ongoing need?
They begin or continue paying What makes the ongoing price worthwhile to them?

That main task needs a definition for each product before its completion becomes a useful signal. Opening a dashboard might only show that registration worked. The meaningful action should reflect what the person wanted to accomplish, and any measurement should collect only the information needed to understand that behavior.

With a small number of users, raw counts and conversations need to sit alongside any percentages. A few people leaving at one step would justify looking at it; it would not give me a reliable explanation of why everyone leaves. The channel context matters too. People arriving from my existing network may behave differently from people encountering the product for the first time.

This could make the next decision more specific. If people understand the offer but cannot finish the task, I have something to investigate in the product. If the people I reach do not recognize the problem, I need to examine the audience or message. Changing both at once would make it harder to understand what helped.

The costs behind the MRR goal

MRR also needs more detail than one rising total. Stripe's explanation of monthly recurring revenue separates growth from new subscriptions and existing customers increasing their subscriptions, and reductions from cancellations or downgrades. Those movements describe different situations that I would want to understand separately.

For example, new subscriptions could increase the total while existing subscribers leave. I would want to see both movements before deciding to repeat the acquisition effort. A larger total on its own would not explain whether the product is keeping the users it already reached.

Then I need to compare recurring revenue with the costs of providing the service. Hosting, payment processing, and support take resources. Where a product uses paid external services, their usage belongs in that calculation too. MRR measures recurring revenue; it does not show what remains after those costs.

The implementation workflow has costs as well, and the time spent helping users has to fit into the week. Even if AI makes an implementation task cheaper for me, I still need to maintain the behavior it introduces and answer questions about it. That is another reason to keep the scope of a growth experiment manageable.

A lifetime deal offered simply to produce early cash would deserve particular scrutiny. An ongoing service creates ongoing work, while a one-time payment has a different revenue shape from a recurring subscription. Before making that offer, I need to understand the support commitment it would create. This is a possible decision to examine; I am not reporting a pricing change to either product.

Ambition needs a reason to continue

The post also encourages builders to aim beyond their first revenue milestone. I like the challenge to think about what a product could become. At the same time, a larger MRR target needs some basis: who else could benefit, how I could reach them, and whether they would keep using it. Changing the number in a goal would leave my current acquisition problem untouched.

For Brainy and MoneyBrain, I want the next milestone to answer one of those questions while leaving room for a bigger ambition.

What I want to do with the next cycle of work

My next useful step would be to give one attempt at finding users the same attention I give an implementation task. Choose a specific audience and problem, make a small attempt to reach them, and leave time to follow up with anyone who tries the product.

A short note for each attempt could record the audience, the message, where I shared it, and what happened afterward. Including the effort spent, even if no money changed hands, would give me something to compare when deciding what to repeat.

For this purpose, focusing on one product at a time would make the follow-up easier to manage. Brainy and MoneyBrain can both remain part of my work, but trying a new audience and message for both simultaneously would divide that attention. AI gives me a way to move implementation forward; I still have to make room in the week to understand the people using the result.

I would set a review point before starting. With a limited budget, I need to consider the time spent as well as the money. Continuing an experiment should depend on what I learn from it; persistence alone would not tell me whether to repeat it, change it, or stop.

That connects two pieces of advice in the screenshot: stay in the game, and consider moving on when the product does not make money. If the goal is a business, revenue and costs need an honest review. Personal usefulness can be a separate reason to maintain it, but it does not establish commercial demand. I want to give a promising idea a fair test without treating every additional month of work as evidence that it will succeed.

I still value the workflow from the previous post. It helps me turn a product idea into software I can review. With Brainy and MoneyBrain, my immediate challenge is to take the next step beyond my LinkedIn circles and learn why someone unfamiliar with me would choose to use what I built.

articles.title: You're Still Optimizing Re-Renders Wrong: The Vue 3 Architecture That Outsmarted the Virtual DOM
articles.description: A visual, 10-minute deep dive into Vue 3 internal architecture. Learn how JavaScript Proxies coordinate with the global targetMap, why Compiler-Informed Block Trees crush traditional brute-force VDOM diffing, how to avoid the destructuring trap, and how Vapor Mode compiles directly to the DOM.
articles.body_html:
If you have built applications in modern frontend frameworks, you have almost certainly encountered the re-render nightmare.

In traditional Virtual DOM architectures, updating a single state variable often causes an entire component tree to re-execute from top to bottom. To prevent performance bottlenecks, developers must manually wrap calculations in memoization hooks, carefully manage dependency arrays, and worry about stale closures:

// The manual dependency tightrope
const userProfile = useMemo(() => {
  return calculateComplexMetrics(user, filters);
}, [user.id, filters.activeStatus]); // Miss a dependency, and your UI breaks

One missing dependency in that array creates subtle, agonizing bugs. One unnecessary dependency triggers expensive cascading re-renders across dozens of child components.

Then you look at Vue 3:

// In Vue 3: No dependency array. No manual memoization.
const userProfile = computed(() => {
  return calculateComplexMetrics(user.value, filters.activeStatus);
});

You mutate user.value.name, and only the exact paragraph rendering that name updates. The parent component does not re-render. Sibling components do not recalculate. There are no dependency arrays, no stale closures, and no manual memoization hooks.

To many developers, this behavior looks like magic or dangerous hidden reactivity.

In reality, Vue 3 is powered by one of the most sophisticated engineering architectures in modern software: a fine-grained Proxy dependency graph coordinated with a Compiler-Informed Block Tree.

Here is how Vue 3 actually tracks state, updates the DOM, and eliminates the re-render cascade.

1. The Reactivity Engine: Proxies, track(), and trigger()

In Vue 2, reactivity was implemented using Object.defineProperty(). The engine recursively traversed every property of your data object on initialization and converted them into getters and setters.

This approach suffered from notorious limitations:

  • Adding a new property (obj.newKey = 123) went undetected, requiring Vue.set().
  • Deleting a property went undetected, requiring Vue.delete().
  • Direct array index mutations (arr[0] = 'new') were unobservable without overriding prototype methods.
  • Deeply nested objects incurred heavy upfront performance costs during initialization.

Vue 3 replaced Object.defineProperty() entirely with modern JavaScript Proxy objects.

The Global Dependency Store (targetMap)

At the core of Vue 3 is a private, module-level data structure named targetMap.

targetMap is a nested multi-level registry that maps objects and their properties to the functions that depend on them:

targetMap (WeakMap)
 └── [target object] ──► depsMap (Map)
                          └── [property key] ──► dep (Set of ReactiveEffects)
  1. targetMap (WeakMap): Holds raw target objects as keys. Because it is a WeakMap, if your application discards the original object, the garbage collector cleans it up automatically, preventing memory leaks.
  2. depsMap (Map): Maps each specific property name of that object (e.g., 'count', 'username') to its dependency tracker.
  3. dep (Set): A Set containing all active ReactiveEffect instances (such as a component render function, a watch callback, or a computed value) that read that specific property.

How track() Registers Dependencies (The Getter Trap)

When you write:

const state = reactive({ count: 0 });

Vue wraps your raw object in a Proxy.

When a component renders, it executes inside a ReactiveEffect wrapper, setting a global pointer named activeEffect to point to that component's render function.

When your template evaluates state.count:

  1. The Proxy's get trap intercepts the property read.
  2. The proxy invokes Vue's internal track(target, 'count') function.
  3. track() checks: Is there currently an activeEffect running?
  4. If yes, it fetches or creates the dep Set for target.count inside targetMap and adds activeEffect to the Set.

You never declare dependency arrays because JavaScript's runtime call stack declares them for you. Any property read while activeEffect is running is automatically recorded as an exact subscriber.

How trigger() Fires Updates (The Setter Trap)

When you execute:

state.count = 42;
  1. The Proxy's set trap intercepts the mutation.
  2. The proxy assigns the new value to the raw underlying object using Reflect.set().
  3. It invokes Vue's internal trigger(target, 'count') function.
  4. trigger() looks up targetMap.get(target).get('count').
  5. It retrieves the Set of subscribed effects and schedules them for execution.

Only the exact components and computed properties subscribed to state.count are scheduled to run. Unrelated components are completely untouched.

2. The Compiler-Informed Virtual DOM: Block Trees and Patch Flags

Virtual DOMs earned a reputation for being heavy and resource-intensive because traditional implementations (like React's standard reconciler) operate on brute-force tree diffing.

In a traditional Virtual DOM:

  • When state changes, the component function executes again.
  • It allocates a brand-new tree of Virtual DOM nodes (VNodes) in memory.
  • The reconciler recursively compares every old VNode with every new VNode, checking tags, props, and children, even if 95% of those nodes are purely static HTML that can never change.

Vue 3 solved this through an architectural breakthrough: the Compiler-Informed Virtual DOM.

The Static Analysis Advantage

Because Vue templates have a deterministic structure, the Vue compiler analyzes your template at build time to identify which parts are dynamic and which parts are static.

Consider this template:

<div class="user-card">
  <header>
    <h1>User Profile</h1>
    <span class="badge">Verified</span>
  </header>
  <p class="bio">{{ user.bio }}</p>
  <button :class="{ active: isActive }">Follow</button>
</div>

In a traditional framework, updating user.bio requires diffing the <div class="user-card">, the <header>, the <h1>, the <span>, and the <button>.

The Vue 3 compiler does something radically different:

1. Static Hoisting

The <header> containing <h1>User Profile</h1> and <span class="badge"> contains zero dynamic bindings.

The compiler pulls those VNodes completely outside the component render function. They are created once when your application loads and reused across every future render. Their memory allocation during updates is zero.

2. Patch Flags (Bitwise Optimization)

For dynamic elements, the compiler attaches a numeric PatchFlag representing precisely what can change:

// Compiled output snippet
_createVNode("p", { class: "bio" }, _toDisplayString(_ctx.user.bio), 1 /* TEXT */)
_createVNode("button", { class: _normalizeClass({ active: _ctx.isActive }) }, "Follow", 2 /* CLASS */)

The number 1 is a bitmask for TEXT. The number 2 is a bitmask for CLASS.

When diffing the <p> tag, Vue performs a single bitwise check (patchFlag & PatchFlags.TEXT). If true, it updates node.textContent directly, skipping any checks for attributes, event listeners, or styles.

3. The Block Tree (dynamicChildren)

The root <div> is compiled into a Block.

A Block maintains a flat array called dynamicChildren. Instead of traversing the nested DOM tree recursively, the Block collects only the dynamic elements:

Block (div.user-card)
 └── dynamicChildren: [
       VNode (p.bio, PatchFlag: 1),
       VNode (button, PatchFlag: 2)
     ]

When user.bio updates, the diffing algorithm does not traverse the tree. It iterates over a flat array of two items!

The diffing cost becomes proportional to the number of dynamic bindings on the page, rather than the total size of your HTML tree.

3. ref() vs reactive(): The Destructuring Trap

One of the most frequent points of confusion for developers adopting Vue 3 is choosing between ref() and reactive().

Both create reactive state, but their underlying implementation mechanisms differ fundamentally.

The Mechanism of ref()

JavaScript primitive types (number, string, boolean, null, undefined) are passed by value, not by reference. You cannot wrap a primitive in a JavaScript Proxy.

To make primitives reactive, Vue introduces the RefImpl class:

class RefImpl {
  private _value;
  public dep = new Set();

  constructor(val) {
    this._value = val;
  }

  get value() {
    trackRefValue(this);
    return this._value;
  }

  set value(newVal) {
    this._value = newVal;
    triggerRefValue(this);
  }
}

A ref() is simply an object with a single property: .value.

Reading .value triggers the getter and tracks dependencies. Mutating .value triggers the setter and notifies subscribers.

Because it is wrapped in an object container, you can pass a ref across composable functions, return it from stores, and pass it as function arguments without losing reactivity.

The Mechanism of reactive()

reactive() accepts an object and wraps it directly in a Proxy.

It feels more natural to write because you do not need to append .value in your script code:

const user = reactive({
  name: "Emma",
  age: 26,
});

user.age++; // Natural syntax

The Destructuring Trap

Here is where thousands of developers run into unexpected silent failures:

// A common fatal mistake
const user = reactive({ name: "Emma", age: 26 });

// Destructuring breaks reactivity!
const { name, age } = user;

Why does destructuring destroy reactivity?

Remember: user is a Proxy intercepting property access on the user object.

When you write const { age } = user, JavaScript evaluates user.age, retrieves the raw primitive number 26, and assigns it to a new local variable named age.

The variable age is now just the plain number 26. It is completely disconnected from the Proxy. When the original user.age mutates later, age remains 26. The Proxy's getter and setter traps are never invoked.

The Solution: toRefs()

If you need to destructure a reactive object, you must convert its properties into individual ref objects using toRefs():

import { reactive, toRefs } from 'vue';

const user = reactive({ name: "Emma", age: 26 });

// toRefs wraps each property in a custom getter/setter proxy pointing back to user
const { name, age } = toRefs(user);

age.value++; // Reactivity is fully preserved!

4. The Batching Engine: Scheduler and nextTick()

What happens if you update a reactive variable fifty times inside a loop?

const count = ref(0);

function runStressTest() {
  for (let i = 0; i < 50; i++) {
    count.value++;
  }
}

Does Vue re-render the DOM fifty times in rapid succession, thrashing the browser layout engine?

No. Vue updates the DOM asynchronously using an internal Scheduler.

The Microtask Queue

When a reactive state change invokes trigger():

  1. Vue does not execute the component's render function immediately.
  2. It passes the render job to queueJob(job).
  3. The scheduler checks if this specific component's render job is already queued. If it is already in the queue, it ignores the duplicate call.
  4. The scheduler flushes the entire job queue in a single batch on the browser's next Microtask tick using Promise.resolve().then(flushJobs).

Regardless of how many times you mutate reactive state synchronously during a function execution, the component's render function runs exactly once.

Accessing Updated DOM via nextTick()

Because DOM updates are queued on a microtask, reading the physical DOM immediately after mutating state returns the old layout:

count.value = 5;
console.log(document.querySelector('.counter').textContent); // Still prints old value!

To wait until the scheduler has completed its microtask flush and committed the updates to the physical DOM, Vue provides nextTick():

import { nextTick } from 'vue';

count.value = 5;
await nextTick();
console.log(document.querySelector('.counter').textContent); // Now prints "5"

nextTick() simply attaches a callback to the exact same microtask promise chain, guaranteeing that your inspection logic runs immediately after the DOM update commits.

5. The Evolution: Vue 2, Vue 3, and Vapor Mode

Frontend framework design is moving away from heavyweight runtime Virtual DOM reconciliation toward compile-time direct DOM operations.

We have seen this trend through frameworks like Svelte and SolidJS.

Vue is uniquely positioned in this landscape because of its architectural progression across three distinct eras:

Era 1: Vue 2 (Runtime Virtual DOM + Object.defineProperty)

  • Relied on ES5 getters and setters.
  • Full-tree recursive Virtual DOM diffing.
  • Required manual workarounds for array mutations and dynamic properties.

Era 2: Vue 3 (Proxy Reactivity + Compiler-Informed Block Trees)

  • Native ES6 Proxies for complete reactivity coverage.
  • Build-time static hoisting, PatchFlags, and Block Trees.
  • Up to 300% faster VDOM reconciliation than traditional brute-force diffing engines.

Era 3: Vue Vapor Mode (Opt-In Direct DOM Compilation)

  • The next major leap in Vue's architecture.
  • For opted-in components, Vapor Mode completely eliminates the Virtual DOM.
  • The template compiler translates your template into fine-grained direct DOM creation and update calls tied directly to reactivity signals: 
// Conceptual Vapor Mode compilation output
import { renderEffect, setText } from 'vue/vapor';

const n0 = document.createElement('h1');
renderEffect(() => {
  setText(n0, count.value);
});

When count.value updates in Vapor Mode:

  • Zero VNodes are allocated in memory.
  • Zero diffing algorithms run.
  • The signal directly triggers setText(n0, count.value) to mutate the physical DOM node in place.

Best of all, Vapor Mode uses the exact same Single-File Component syntax (<template>, <script setup>). You do not need to learn a new templating language or rewrite existing components to benefit from zero-VDOM performance.

6. Three Common Vue Reactivity Traps

Understanding Vue's internal architecture immediately arms you against the three most frustrating pitfalls developers encounter:

Trap 1: Storing Heavy External Objects in reactive()

If you store non-primitive third-party objects (such as a Three.js scene, a Monaco Editor instance, a Chart.js canvas, or a Mapbox map) inside a standard reactive() or ref():

// DANGEROUS: Destroys performance
const editorInstance = ref(monaco.editor.create(...));

Vue will recursively wrap the thousands of internal properties, prototypes, and event listeners of that third-party library in reactive Proxies. This creates massive memory overhead and frequently causes third-party libraries to crash when their internal this contexts are proxied.

The Fix: Use shallowRef() or markRaw():

import { shallowRef } from 'vue';

// Safe: Only the .value pointer is reactive; inner properties are untouched
const editorInstance = shallowRef(monaco.editor.create(...));

Trap 2: Infinite Watch Loops

Because Vue tracks dependencies automatically during execution, creating circular reads and writes inside watchEffect() will crash your application:

// CRASHES: Maximum recursive update cycle exceeded
watchEffect(() => {
  total.value = items.value.length;
  // If reading total somewhere triggers items to update, an infinite loop ensues
});

The Fix: Prefer explicit computed() for derived state, and reserve watchEffect() strictly for side effects (such as making API calls or updating local storage).

Trap 3: Direct Mutation of Props

In Vue, data flow is strictly unidirectional. Passing a reactive object as a prop and mutating it directly in a child component bypasses parent state tracking and leads to unpredictable rendering inconsistencies.

The Fix: Emit events using defineEmits() or use v-model with defineModel() to maintain clear ownership over state mutations.

The Mental Shift

The difference between struggling with frontend performance and building scalable interfaces comes down to your mental model:

Stop thinking of reactive components as functions that need to re-execute repeatedly from top to bottom.

Vue 3 is an event-driven signal graph paired with an intelligent compiler.

  • State is a Proxy network, registering dependencies automatically on access.
  • Templates are Block Trees, diffing only the slots marked with PatchFlags.
  • DOM updates are batched asynchronously through microtask queues.
  • And with Vapor Mode, the Virtual DOM step disappears entirely, connecting state directly to DOM nodes.

Once you understand this architecture, the need for complex memoization hooks disappears, re-render cascades vanish, and building reactive user interfaces becomes natural, predictable, and exceptionally fast.
