How has Vue's fine-grained reactivity model influenced how you design your frontend state? Have you experienced the performance shift between traditional re-render engines and Proxy-based tracking, or experimented with early Vapor Mode builds? Share your thoughts and architecture experiences in the comments below.

articles.title: 20 Linux Commands Every DevOps Engineer Needs to Know
articles.description: Straight to the point:            1. man – Understanding Linux Commands   One thing you will quickly...
articles.body_html:
Straight to the point:

1. man – Understanding Linux Commands

One thing you will quickly discover when working with Linux is that there are many commands, and each command comes with different options and ways of using it.

You don't have to memorise everything. Linux provides manual pages (man pages) that explain how commands work, their available options, and their usage.

For example:

man ls

This opens the manual page for the ls command.

You can navigate through the manual using the arrow keys or Page Up and Page Down. When you are done, press q to quit.

This is particularly useful when working on servers where you may not have access to a browser or when you need to understand an option before using it.

2. sudo – Running Commands with Elevated Privileges

In Linux, not every user has permission to perform every operation.

For example, installing software, modifying certain system files, and managing system services usually require administrative privileges.

This is where sudo comes in.

sudo apt install nginx

The command runs with elevated privileges, allowing you to install Nginx on your system.

You may also come across:

sudo su

This opens a root shell, allowing you to run multiple commands with administrative privileges.

However, I would recommend using sudo for individual commands rather than staying logged in as root for prolonged periods. Running everything as root increases the risk of accidentally modifying or deleting important system files.

To leave a root shell, run:

exit

3. pwd – Knowing Your Current Location

Have you ever navigated through several directories and suddenly forgotten where you are?

The pwd command solves that problem.

It stands for Print Working Directory and displays the full path of your current location.

pwd

Example output:

/home/michael/DevOps

When managing servers, you will often move between application directories, configuration folders, log directories, and other system locations.

Knowing your current directory helps you avoid running commands against the wrong files or folders.

4. ls – Listing Files and Directories

The ls command allows you to see the files and directories in your current location.

ls

However, there are a few options that make it more useful.

ls -l

Displays files in a detailed format, including permissions, ownership, file size, and modification dates.

ls -a

Displays hidden files and directories, including files such as .bashrc and .ssh.

ls -lah

Combines the options to show hidden files, detailed information, and human-readable file sizes.

This is one of the commands you will use regularly when inspecting application directories, checking configuration files, and investigating file permissions.

5. cd – Navigating Between Directories

The cd command allows you to change your current directory.

For example:

cd /var/www

This moves you into the /var/www directory.

To move one directory backwards:

cd ..

To move up two levels:

cd ../..

You can also return to your home directory by running:

cd ~

One small habit worth developing is using the Tab key for autocomplete. Instead of typing an entire directory name, start typing the first few characters and press Tab.

It saves time and reduces mistakes, especially when working with long directory paths.

6. mkdir – Creating Directories

The mkdir command allows you to create directories.

For example:

mkdir DevOps

This creates a directory called DevOps in your current location.

You can also create multiple directories at once:

mkdir logs backups scripts

Another useful option is -p, which allows you to create nested directories even when the parent directories do not exist.

mkdir -p /var/www/myapp/logs

You will find this useful when preparing server environments and organising application files.

7. touch – Creating Files

While mkdir creates directories, touch can create empty files.

touch app.py

This creates an empty file called app.py.

You can also create several files at once:

touch Dockerfile requirements.txt .env

An important detail is that touch does not overwrite the contents of an existing file. It updates its timestamps instead.

You will often use it when creating configuration files, scripts, and other application files.

8. cp – Copying Files and Directories

The cp command allows you to copy files from one location to another.

For example:

cp app.py backups/

This creates a copy of app.py inside the backups directory while leaving the original file in place.

To copy an entire directory and its contents, use the recursive option:

cp -r myapp backups/

This can be useful when creating backups of configuration files or application directories before making changes.

9. mv – Moving and Renaming Files

The mv command is used to move files and directories from one location to another.

For example:

mv app.py /var/www/myapp/

This moves the file into the specified directory.

You can also use mv to rename files:

mv old_config.conf new_config.conf

Unlike cp, mv does not leave a second copy behind.

When working with Linux servers, you may use it to organise application files, move configuration files, or rename files during deployment.

Be careful when moving files into directories where another file has the same name, as it may replace the existing file.

10. rm – Removing Files and Directories

The rm command allows you to delete files.

rm app.py

To remove a directory and everything inside it, you can use:

rm -r myapp

You may also encounter:

rm -rf myapp

Here, -r means recursive, while -f forces removal without prompting for confirmation in many situations.

Be very careful with this command.

A wrong path can result in deleting important application files, configuration files, or even critical system data.

Always check your current directory using pwd and inspect the target using ls before running destructive commands. Avoid running recursive deletion commands with sudo unless you fully understand what you are removing.

11. cat – Reading File Contents

The cat command allows you to display the contents of a file directly in the terminal.

cat config.txt

This is particularly useful when checking configuration files or reading application settings.

For example:

cat /etc/hosts

Displays the contents of the system's hosts file.

You can also combine cat with other commands using a pipe.

cat config.txt | grep "DATABASE"

This displays only the lines containing the word DATABASE.

For very large files, commands such as less are often more convenient because they allow you to navigate through the contents without printing everything at once.

12. echo – Printing and Writing Text

The echo command prints text to the terminal.

echo "Hello DevOps"

However, it is also useful when writing information into files and working with environment variables.

For example:

echo "Hello DevOps" > message.txt

The > operator writes the text into the file. If the file already exists, its previous contents will be replaced.

To append instead of replacing the contents, use >>.

echo "Learning Linux commands" >> message.txt

You can also use echo to check environment variables.

echo $HOME
echo $PATH

This becomes useful when troubleshooting application environments, checking configuration values, and working with deployment scripts.

One important thing: avoid using echo to write secrets into shell commands or scripts that may end up in shell history or logs.

13. grep – Searching Through Files

Imagine you are working on a server and have a configuration file containing hundreds of lines. You want to find a particular setting without reading everything.

This is where grep becomes useful.

For example:

grep "DATABASE" .env

This searches for lines containing DATABASE in the .env file.

You can also search recursively through directories:

grep -r "DEBUG" /var/www/myapp/

Some useful options include:

  • -i ignores uppercase and lowercase differences.
  • -n displays line numbers.
  • -r searches recursively through directories.
  • -v displays lines that do not match the search.

For example:

grep -in "error" application.log

This searches for the word error, regardless of case, and displays the matching line numbers.

For DevOps engineers, grep is particularly useful when investigating application logs, checking configuration files, and troubleshooting deployment issues.

14. find – Finding Files and Directories

The find command allows you to search for files and directories based on their names, types, sizes, modification times, and other conditions.

For example:

find /var/www -name "Dockerfile"

This searches the /var/www directory and its subdirectories for files named Dockerfile.

To find all files ending in .log:

find /var/log -type f -name "*.log"

To find directories:

find /var/www -type d

Unlike locate, which searches an indexed database, find searches the specified directory tree directly.

This is useful when investigating where application files are stored, locating configuration files, and identifying old files that may need attention.

You may also encounter locate, which can quickly search for files by name using a pre-built index. Its database may need updating before newly created files appear.

15. history – Viewing Previously Executed Commands

The history command displays commands you have previously executed in your terminal.

history

This can be particularly useful when you have forgotten a command you ran earlier or want to repeat a previous operation.

You can search through your command history using:

history | grep "docker"

You may also execute a previous command using its history number:

!25

This executes command number 25 from your history.

You can configure Bash to display timestamps alongside your command history:

export HISTTIMEFORMAT="%d-%m-%Y %T "

This makes it easier to see when commands were executed, provided the shell has recorded the relevant timestamps.

However, remember that shell history is not a complete audit log. Commands may not be recorded, and it should not be treated as a reliable security record.

16. chmod – Managing File Permissions

Linux uses permissions to control who can read, write, and execute files and directories.

There are three main permission types:

  • Read (r): Allows a user to read a file.
  • Write (w): Allows a user to modify a file.
  • Execute (x): Allows a user to execute a file or access a directory.

These permissions are assigned to three categories:

  • Owner: The user who owns the file.
  • Group: Users belonging to the assigned group.
  • Others: Everyone else.

The chmod command allows us to modify these permissions.

For example:

chmod 755 deploy.sh

This gives the owner read, write, and execute permissions, while the group and others receive read and execute permissions.

Another example:

chmod 644 config.txt

This gives the owner read and write permissions, while the group and others can only read the file.

You can also use:

chmod +x deploy.sh

This adds execute permission without replacing the other existing permissions.

This is particularly useful when working with deployment scripts, application files, and server configuration.

A common mistake is using chmod 777 on everything because an application is having permission issues. This gives everyone read, write, and execute permissions, which can create serious security problems. It is better to understand the actual permission requirement and assign only what is necessary.

17. chown – Changing File Ownership

While chmod manages permissions, chown allows you to change the ownership of files and directories.

For example:

sudo chown michael app.py

This changes the owner of app.py to michael.

You can also change both the owner and group:

sudo chown michael:developers app.py

To apply the change recursively to a directory and its contents:

sudo chown -R michael:developers /var/www/myapp

This is especially useful when deploying applications.

For example, if an application runs under a particular Linux user, the application files may need to be owned by that user or a suitable group.

Understanding the difference between ownership and permissions is important when troubleshooting issues such as applications being unable to read configuration files or write to log directories.

18. useradd – Creating Linux Users

Linux allows you to create different user accounts with different permissions and access levels.

The useradd command is used to create new users.

For example:

sudo useradd michael

This creates a user account called michael.

If you want to create a user with a home directory and an interactive Bash shell, you can use:

sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash michael

You can then set the user's password using:

sudo passwd michael

Another useful command is groupadd, which creates a new group.

sudo groupadd developers

You can add an existing user to that group using usermod:

sudo usermod -aG developers michael

The -aG options append the user to the specified supplementary group without removing their existing supplementary group memberships.

These commands are useful when managing server access, separating responsibilities, and ensuring that different users have only the permissions they need.

19. apt – Installing and Managing Software

Most Linux distributions have a package manager that helps you install, update, and remove software.

On Ubuntu and other Debian-based distributions, one of the package managers you will frequently encounter is APT.

To update the package information from configured repositories, run:

sudo apt update

To upgrade installed packages:

sudo apt upgrade

To install a package:

sudo apt install nginx

To remove a package:

sudo apt remove nginx

You can also install multiple packages in one command:

sudo apt install nginx docker.io git curl

As a DevOps engineer, you will regularly install and configure software such as Nginx, Docker, Git, Python, and other server dependencies.

Understanding package management is important because keeping software updated is part of maintaining a secure and reliable server.

Note that APT is used on Debian-based distributions. Other Linux distributions use different package managers, such as dnf on Fedora and many RHEL-based systems.

20. systemctl – Managing Linux Services

This is one of the commands I consider particularly important for anyone working with Linux servers.

Linux runs several background services that perform different tasks. These may include web servers, databases, SSH, monitoring agents, and other application services.

On most modern Linux distributions using systemd, systemctl is used to manage these services.

For example, to check the status of Nginx:

sudo systemctl status nginx

To start a service:

sudo systemctl start nginx

To stop it:

sudo systemctl stop nginx

To restart it:

sudo systemctl restart nginx

To make a service start automatically when the server boots:

sudo systemctl enable nginx

You can also check whether a service is enabled:

sudo systemctl is-enabled nginx

Imagine you have deployed a Django application behind Nginx and Gunicorn. If your website suddenly stops responding, checking the status of these services is one of the first things you may want to do.

For example:

sudo systemctl status nginx
sudo systemctl status gunicorn

Understanding how to manage services is an important part of server administration and application troubleshooting.

Other Commands Worth Learning

The 20 commands above provide a good starting point, but there are several others from the book that I would recommend adding to your learning list.

For processing command output:

awk
cut
xargs
  • awk helps extract specific columns or process structured text.
  • cut extracts specific characters or fields from lines of text.
  • xargs takes input from one command and passes it as arguments to another.

For example:

who | awk '{print $1}'

This extracts the usernames from the output of who.

cut -d: -f1 /etc/passwd

This extracts the first field from each line of the Linux user account file.

For monitoring and troubleshooting:

ps aux
top
df -h
du -sh /var/log
free -h
ss -tulpn

These are particularly important for DevOps work.

  • ps aux displays running processes.
  • top provides a live view of system processes and resource usage.
  • df -h shows available and used disk space across mounted filesystems.
  • du -sh shows the size of a directory or file.
  • free -h displays memory usage.
  • ss -tulpn helps inspect listening network sockets and associated processes (some process details require elevated privileges).

For example, if an application stops responding, you may need to investigate whether the server has run out of memory, whether a process has stopped, or whether the required network port is listening.

For reading logs:

journalctl -u nginx

This displays logs for the Nginx service managed by systemd.

To follow new log entries as they appear:

journalctl -u nginx -f

This is useful when investigating why a service failed or monitoring what happens after restarting an application.

Final Thoughts

Learning Linux commands is not about memorising hundreds of commands or trying to become an expert in every available option. It is about understanding what you are trying to achieve and knowing which tools can help you get there.

As a DevOps engineer, you will spend a considerable amount of time working with servers, deploying applications, managing services, checking logs, configuring permissions, and troubleshooting problems.

You may not use every command every day, but you should be comfortable navigating the terminal and knowing where to look when something goes wrong. My advice is to practise these commands on an Ubuntu virtual machine or a Linux environment using WSL. Create files, move them around, install packages, create users, change permissions, and inspect running services.

Don't just read the commands. Use them.

The more comfortable you become with the Linux terminal, the easier it becomes to work with Docker, CI/CD pipelines, cloud infrastructure, and other DevOps tools.

articles.title: TypeScript `keyof typeof` in 2026: Practical Patterns for Enum-Like Objects and Config Maps
articles.description: Master keyof typeof to build type-safe config objects, route maps, and registries. Learn when this pattern beats enums and where runtime validation takes over.
articles.body_html:
TypeScript keyof typeof in 2026: Practical Patterns for Enum-Like Objects and Config Maps

This article was written with the assistance of AI, under human supervision and review.

TypeScript's keyof typeof pattern surfaces when teams need compile-time safety for object keys without the runtime cost or API surface of enums. Config objects and route maps break silently when developers reference nonexistent keys, and traditional string unions require manual duplication. The pattern extracts keys directly from the object's shape, but combining keyof and typeof trips engineers who have not traced what each operator returns.

const API_ROUTES = {
  users: "/api/users",
  posts: "/api/posts",
  auth: "/api/auth"
};

function fetchData(endpoint: string) {
  return fetch(API_ROUTES[endpoint]); // No type safety
}

fetchData("user"); // Typo goes undetected

Problem flow showing unsafe string access leading to runtime error

Teams apply keyof typeof to constrain the parameter to valid keys only.

const API_ROUTES = {
  users: "/api/users",
  posts: "/api/posts",
  auth: "/api/auth"
} as const;

type RouteKey = keyof typeof API_ROUTES;

function fetchData(endpoint: RouteKey) {
  return fetch(API_ROUTES[endpoint]);
}

fetchData("users"); // OK
fetchData("user");  // Compile error: Type '"user"' is not assignable to type 'RouteKey'

Solution flow showing type-safe key access caught at compile time

This post demonstrates when keyof typeof solves real problems, when enums remain a better fit, and where runtime validation becomes essential.

Key Takeaways

  • keyof typeof extracts object keys as a union type without manual duplication, enabling type-safe access to config objects and registries.
  • The pattern works best for static objects known at compile time; dynamic or fetched data requires runtime schema validation instead.
  • Real enums offer reverse mappings and namespace pollution; as const objects with keyof typeof keep the codebase closer to standard JavaScript.
  • Combining keyof typeof with as const prevents widening and ensures the narrowest possible key types.
  • Exhaustive type checking with never catches missing registry entries at compile time when all keys must be handled.

Understanding keyof and typeof Separately Before Combining Them

The keyof operator produces a union of an object type's keys.

type User = {
  id: number;
  name: string;
  email: string;
};

type UserKeys = keyof User; // "id" | "name" | "email"

The typeof operator extracts the type of a value.

const config = {
  apiUrl: "https://api.example.com",
  timeout: 5000
};

type ConfigType = typeof config;
// { apiUrl: string; timeout: number; }

When developers write keyof config, TypeScript raises an error because keyof operates on types, not values. The config variable holds a value. The typeof operator bridges the gap by deriving the type from the value, then keyof extracts the keys from that derived type.

const config = {
  apiUrl: "https://api.example.com",
  timeout: 5000
};

type ConfigKeys = keyof typeof config; // "apiUrl" | "timeout"

Each operator addresses a distinct problem. The typeof operator answers "what is the type of this value?" and keyof answers "what are the valid keys of this type?" Combining them solves "what keys can this value accept?" without writing a separate type definition.

According to the TypeScript 2.9 release notes, keyof now includes number and symbol keys alongside string keys. The union string | number | symbol reflects all property key types JavaScript supports. Object types with numeric index signatures yield number in their keyof result.

type Arrayish = {
  length: number;
  [x: number]: string;
};

type ArrayishKeys = keyof Arrayish; // "length" | number

This matters when config objects use numeric enum keys or computed symbol properties. The pattern captures those keys without special handling.

TypeScript compiler checking keyof typeof pattern

Practical Pattern: Type-Safe Config Objects and Route Maps

Config objects store application constants: API endpoints, feature flags, theme tokens. Developers reference these values throughout the codebase. A typo in a string key surfaces only at runtime when the lookup returns undefined.

const FEATURE_FLAGS = {
  darkMode: true,
  betaFeatures: false,
  analytics: true
};

function isEnabled(flag: string): boolean {
  return FEATURE_FLAGS[flag] ?? false;
}

if (isEnabled("darkmode")) { // Typo: lowercase 'm'
  // Silently returns false instead of true
}

The keyof typeof pattern constrains the parameter to valid keys.

const FEATURE_FLAGS = {
  darkMode: true,
  betaFeatures: false,
  analytics: true
} as const;

type FeatureFlag = keyof typeof FEATURE_FLAGS;

function isEnabled(flag: FeatureFlag): boolean {
  return FEATURE_FLAGS[flag];
}

if (isEnabled("darkMode")) { // OK
  // Correctly returns true
}

if (isEnabled("darkmode")) { // Compile error
  // Type '"darkmode"' is not assignable to type 'FeatureFlag'
}

The as const assertion prevents TypeScript from widening true to boolean. Without it, FEATURE_FLAGS has type { darkMode: boolean; betaFeatures: boolean; analytics: boolean }, and the values become mutable booleans. The as const assertion locks the object to readonly literal types.

Route maps follow the same pattern. Applications maintain a central registry of paths.

const ROUTES = {
  home: "/",
  profile: "/profile",
  settings: "/settings",
  admin: "/admin/dashboard"
} as const;

type Route = keyof typeof ROUTES;

function navigate(route: Route): void {
  window.location.href = ROUTES[route];
}

navigate("settings"); // OK
navigate("setting");  // Compile error

This pattern scales to nested config objects. Teams often organize settings by domain.

const CONFIG = {
  api: {
    baseUrl: "https://api.example.com",
    timeout: 5000,
    retries: 3
  },
  ui: {
    theme: "dark",
    language: "en"
  }
} as const;

type TopLevelKey = keyof typeof CONFIG; // "api" | "ui"
type ApiKey = keyof typeof CONFIG.api;  // "baseUrl" | "timeout" | "retries"

function getApiSetting(key: ApiKey) {
  return CONFIG.api[key];
}

The pattern eliminates drift between the object shape and the type definition. When developers add a new route or flag, the type updates automatically.

Enum-Like Objects: When to Use keyof typeof vs Real Enums

TypeScript enums generate runtime objects and provide reverse mappings. Numeric enums map keys to values and values back to keys. According to the official enums documentation, the following enum compiles to bidirectional mappings.

enum LogLevel {
  ERROR,
  WARN,
  INFO,
  DEBUG
}

console.log(LogLevel.ERROR);    // 0
console.log(LogLevel[0]);       // "ERROR"

String enums do not generate reverse mappings. The compiled output stores only the forward mapping from key to value. Enums also pollute the namespace: every key becomes a global identifier at compile time and a property at runtime.

enum Status {
  Active = "ACTIVE",
  Inactive = "INACTIVE"
}

// Compiled output (simplified):
var Status;
(function (Status) {
  Status["Active"] = "ACTIVE";
  Status["Inactive"] = "INACTIVE";
})(Status || (Status = {}));

The keyof typeof pattern with as const objects produces similar type safety without runtime overhead.

const Status = {
  Active: "ACTIVE",
  Inactive: "INACTIVE"
} as const;

type StatusKey = keyof typeof Status;     // "Active" | "Inactive"
type StatusValue = typeof Status[StatusKey]; // "ACTIVE" | "INACTIVE"

function setStatus(status: StatusValue) {
  console.log(status);
}

setStatus("ACTIVE"); // OK
setStatus("active"); // Compile error

The comparison table shows when each approach fits.

Feature Enum as const + keyof typeof
Reverse mapping (numeric) Yes No
Reverse mapping (string) No No
Runtime object generated Yes Yes (but standard object)
Namespace pollution Yes (global enum identifier) No
Alignment with JavaScript No (TypeScript-specific) Yes
Compile-time key safety Yes Yes
Works with isolatedModules Const enums break Yes

Enums make sense when developers need reverse lookups or when the domain naturally groups related constants under a single namespace. The TypeScript compiler options reference notes that const enums inline values at compile time, but this breaks when isolatedModules is enabled (common in bundler-based projects). The as const object avoids this pitfall.

Comparison of enum vs as const object compilation and runtime behavior

Teams leaning toward standard JavaScript prefer as const objects. Projects requiring reverse mappings or existing enum codebases continue using enums. The choice depends on whether the runtime cost and namespace pollution justify the reverse-mapping feature.

Building Registry Objects with Exhaustive Type Checking

Registries map identifiers to handlers, validators, or configuration blocks. Plugin systems and event dispatchers rely on registries. When developers add a new plugin type, the registry must include a handler for that type. Missing handlers cause runtime failures.

const PLUGIN_TYPES = {
  auth: "authentication",
  cache: "caching",
  logger: "logging"
} as const;

type PluginType = keyof typeof PLUGIN_TYPES;

const pluginHandlers = {
  auth: (config: unknown) => { /* ... */ },
  cache: (config: unknown) => { /* ... */ }
  // Missing 'logger' handler
};

function initializePlugin(type: PluginType, config: unknown) {
  const handler = pluginHandlers[type];
  if (!handler) {
    throw new Error(`No handler for plugin type: ${type}`);
  }
  handler(config);
}

The runtime check catches the missing handler, but only when code paths execute. Exhaustive type checking surfaces the gap at compile time. The never type represents values that should not exist. When developers assign a value to never, TypeScript raises an error unless the value is genuinely unreachable.

const PLUGIN_TYPES = {
  auth: "authentication",
  cache: "caching",
  logger: "logging"
} as const;

type PluginType = keyof typeof PLUGIN_TYPES;

const pluginHandlers: Record<PluginType, (config: unknown) => void> = {
  auth: (config) => { /* ... */ },
  cache: (config) => { /* ... */ },
  logger: (config) => { /* ... */ }
};

function initializePlugin(type: PluginType, config: unknown) {
  const handler = pluginHandlers[type];
  handler(config);
}

The Record<PluginType, ...> type requires every key in PluginType to appear in pluginHandlers. If developers add a new plugin type to PLUGIN_TYPES but forget the corresponding handler, the compiler raises an error.

const PLUGIN_TYPES = {
  auth: "authentication",
  cache: "caching",
  logger: "logging",
  metrics: "metrics" // New plugin type
} as const;

type PluginType = keyof typeof PLUGIN_TYPES;

const pluginHandlers: Record<PluginType, (config: unknown) => void> = {
  auth: (config) => { /* ... */ },
  cache: (config) => { /* ... */ },
  logger: (config) => { /* ... */ }
  // Compile error: Property 'metrics' is missing in type
};

This pattern extends to switch statements. When all cases are handled, the default branch becomes unreachable. Assigning the unhandled value to never catches missing cases.

function processPlugin(type: PluginType) {
  switch (type) {
    case "auth":
      return "Initializing auth plugin";
    case "cache":
      return "Initializing cache plugin";
    case "logger":
      return "Initializing logger plugin";
    default:
      const exhaustiveCheck: never = type;
      throw new Error(`Unhandled plugin type: ${exhaustiveCheck}`);
  }
}

If developers add a new plugin type without updating the switch statement, the default case assigns the new type to never, and TypeScript raises an error. This pattern enforces completeness across the codebase.

Registry pattern flow showing exhaustive type checking preventing missing handlers

Registry object with exhaustive type checking

Runtime Validation: Where keyof typeof Breaks Down and Schema Validators Take Over

The keyof typeof pattern provides compile-time safety for static objects. When data originates from external sources (API responses, user input, environment variables), the object shape is unknown at compile time. TypeScript cannot verify that runtime data matches the expected structure.

const VALID_ROLES = {
  admin: "ADMIN",
  editor: "EDITOR",
  viewer: "VIEWER"
} as const;

type Role = keyof typeof VALID_ROLES;

async function fetchUserRole(): Promise<Role> {
  const response = await fetch("/api/user/role");
  const data = await response.json();
  return data.role; // No guarantee this is a valid Role
}

The function signature promises to return a Role, but the API could return any string. TypeScript trusts the type annotation. If the API returns "moderator", the application receives an invalid role without warning. Runtime validation bridges the gap.

Schema validators (Zod, Valibot, io-ts) define the expected shape and verify runtime data against it. When validation fails, the library throws or returns an error. When validation succeeds, TypeScript infers the validated type.

import { z } from "zod";

const VALID_ROLES = {
  admin: "ADMIN",
  editor: "EDITOR",
  viewer: "VIEWER"
} as const;

const RoleSchema = z.enum(["admin", "editor", "viewer"]);

type Role = z.infer<typeof RoleSchema>;

async function fetchUserRole(): Promise<Role> {
  const response = await fetch("/api/user/role");
  const data = await response.json();
  const validated = RoleSchema.parse(data.role); // Throws if invalid
  return validated;
}

The z.enum schema accepts only the specified strings. If data.role contains an unexpected value, parse throws a ZodError. The validated value has type Role, and TypeScript guarantees it matches one of the allowed values. Teams often derive the schema from the as const object to maintain a single source of truth.

const VALID_ROLES = {
  admin: "ADMIN",
  editor: "EDITOR",
  viewer: "VIEWER"
} as const;

type Role = keyof typeof VALID_ROLES;

const roleKeys = Object.keys(VALID_ROLES) as Array<Role>;
const RoleSchema = z.enum(roleKeys as [Role, ...Role[]]);

This keeps the object definition as the canonical source. The schema derives from it automatically. When developers add a new role, both the compile-time type and the runtime validator update.

The comparison table shows when to use each approach.

Data source Use keyof typeof Use runtime validation
Hardcoded config Yes No
API responses No Yes
User input No Yes
Environment variables No (or combine with parse) Yes
Internal module exports Yes No
Database query results No Yes

When data crosses trust boundaries (user input, network calls, file reads), validation becomes essential. The keyof typeof pattern cannot protect against malformed or malicious data. Schema validators provide both type safety and runtime guarantees.

Flow showing where compile-time safety ends and runtime validation begins

Advanced Pattern: Combining keyof typeof with as const for Maximum Type Safety

The as const assertion narrows object types to their most specific form. Without it, TypeScript infers mutable types. Combining as const with keyof typeof produces the narrowest possible key types.

const STATUS_CODES = {
  success: 200,
  created: 201,
  badRequest: 400,
  notFound: 404
};

type StatusCodeKey = keyof typeof STATUS_CODES; // Works, but values are number

const strictResponse = (code: StatusCodeKey) => {
  return STATUS_CODES[code]; // Type: number
};

Adding as const locks the values to literal types.

const STATUS_CODES = {
  success: 200,
  created: 201,
  badRequest: 400,
  notFound: 404
} as const;

type StatusCodeKey = keyof typeof STATUS_CODES;
type StatusCodeValue = typeof STATUS_CODES[StatusCodeKey]; // 200 | 201 | 400 | 404

const strictResponse = (code: StatusCodeKey) => {
  return STATUS_CODES[code]; // Type: 200 | 201 | 400 | 404
};

The return type narrows from number to the exact union of status codes. This precision prevents accidental assignment of invalid values.

const STATUS_CODES = {
  success: 200,
  created: 201,
  badRequest: 400,
  notFound: 404
} as const;

type StatusCodeValue = typeof STATUS_CODES[keyof typeof STATUS_CODES];

function handleResponse(code: StatusCodeValue) {
  if (code === 200) {
    // TypeScript knows code is exactly 200
  }
}

handleResponse(200); // OK
handleResponse(500); // Compile error: Argument of type '500' is not assignable

This pattern extends to nested objects. The as const assertion applies recursively to all nested properties.

const CONFIG = {
  endpoints: {
    users: "/api/users",
    posts: "/api/posts"
  },
  limits: {
    pageSize: 20,
    maxRetries: 3
  }
} as const;

type EndpointKey = keyof typeof CONFIG.endpoints; // "users" | "posts"
type Endpoint = typeof CONFIG.endpoints[EndpointKey]; // "/api/users" | "/api/posts"

function callEndpoint(key: EndpointKey): Endpoint {
  return CONFIG.endpoints[key];
}

When developers omit as const, TypeScript infers string for the endpoint values. The narrower literal types provide stronger guarantees and better autocomplete in editors.

Another advanced pattern combines keyof typeof with mapped types to transform object shapes.

const API_METHODS = {
  getUser: "GET",
  createUser: "POST",
  updateUser: "PUT",
  deleteUser: "DELETE"
} as const;

type ApiMethod = keyof typeof API_METHODS;

type ApiHandlers = {
  [K in ApiMethod]: (id: string) => Promise<void>;
};

const handlers: ApiHandlers = {
  getUser: async (id) => { /* ... */ },
  createUser: async (id) => { /* ... */ },
  updateUser: async (id) => { /* ... */ },
  deleteUser: async (id) => { /* ... */ }
};

The mapped type enforces that every method in API_METHODS has a corresponding handler. Adding a new method to the object requires adding a handler, or TypeScript raises an error. This pattern scales to complex registries where each key maps to a different handler signature.

Frequently Asked Questions

When should developers use keyof typeof instead of manually defining a union type?

Use keyof typeof when the object already exists and serves as the source of truth. Manual unions require duplication: developers maintain both the object and the type. When developers add a new key, they must update both locations. The keyof typeof pattern derives the type from the object automatically, eliminating drift.

Does keyof typeof work with class instances or only plain objects?

The pattern works with class instances, but the result includes all public properties and methods, not just data properties. TypeScript extracts keys from the class type, which includes methods. For plain data objects, use as const objects. For classes, consider defining an explicit type or interface that describes only the data properties.

Can keyof typeof extract keys from imported modules?

Yes. When a module exports an object, keyof typeof extracts its keys. Import the object, then apply the operators: type Keys = keyof typeof importedObject. This works across module boundaries. The imported object must be a value (not just a type) because typeof operates on values.

How does keyof typeof interact with TypeScript's strict mode?

The pattern functions identically in strict and non-strict modes. Strict mode enforces stricter null checks and type inference, but keyof typeof behavior remains unchanged. However, strict mode often surfaces additional errors in surrounding code (such as nullable property access), which improves overall type safety when using this pattern.

What happens when the object has optional or nullable properties?

Optional properties appear in the keyof result because they are valid keys on the object type. The key union includes all declared properties, regardless of optionality. When accessing an optional property, TypeScript infers the value type as T | undefined. Use non-null assertions or optional chaining when the property might be absent at runtime.

Conclusion

The keyof typeof pattern provides compile-time safety for static config objects, route maps, and registries without the runtime cost or namespace pollution of enums. Teams apply this pattern when the object shape is known at build time and developers need to constrain code to valid keys. Combining as const with keyof typeof produces the narrowest types and prevents accidental mutations. When data crosses trust boundaries (APIs, user input), runtime validation with schema libraries becomes essential because keyof typeof cannot verify runtime shapes. Exhaustive checking with Record types and never ensures registries remain complete when developers add new entries. The pattern aligns TypeScript codebases with standard JavaScript while maintaining strong type guarantees.

articles.title: Darkroom Heist: turning a darkroom timer into a daily safe-cracking game
articles.description: I bought an old GraLab darkroom timer: a big analog dial built for timing photo prints under a red...
articles.body_html:
I bought an old GraLab darkroom timer: a big analog dial built for timing photo prints under a red safelight. The first time I turned that knob I thought: this is a safe dial.

The plan is to gut it into a game controller (encoder behind the dial, a Pico inside, the toggle as a button). But before soldering anything, I wanted to know if the game was actually fun. So I built it for the web first.

🔐 Play it: haugf.com/vault. A new vault every night at midnight.

The game in 10 seconds

  • 3 tumblers, 60 seconds. Turn slowly and feel for the thunk: one click heavier than the rest, plus a buzz on your phone. Then lock it in.
  • The guard. You hear footsteps, the door opens, and you freeze. Move while he's looking and you're spotted (−10s). Three strikes and you're busted.
  • Daily, like Wordle. Everyone gets the same vault. Your first run is the official one, and after that it's practice.

Design before code

My one rule: mock it first, then build it. The times I jumped straight to code were the times I redid work.

  • One phone screen, no scrolling. LOCK sits in the thumb zone.
  • Stay in the darkroom. Black, safelight red. Run out of time and your print burns.
  • Make it shareable. Wordle's grid is why people post it, so this has one: 
🫆 Darkroom Heist #1
💰 38.2s · Safecracker
🟥🟥🟩
🟩
💰
haugf.com/vault

🟩 crack · 🟥 bad lock · 🔦 spotted · 💰 the final crack

How it's built

One HTML file. No framework, no build step.

Piece How
Daily vault Date-seeded RNG, so everyone gets the same vault and there's no server
Dial <canvas> with touch drag, mouse wheel and arrow keys
Sound All synthesized with Web Audio, no audio files
Haptics navigator.vibrate
Hosting S3 + CloudFront

iOS gotcha: the sound didn't start until your first LOCK press, because iOS only unlocks Web Audio after a tap. The fix is to unlock it on any touch with a silent buffer.

Launching it at a hackathon

I was coaching MakeCU (Columbia's hackathon) and told the room to play for a shirt. CloudFront logs from the first weekend:

  • 57 visitors, 86 game loads
  • 40 of 57 on iPhone
  • 48 came from links tapped in group chats
  • Sunday, with no hackathon push: 26 new players

What playtesters told me:

  • Too much scrolling. → the one-screen layout
  • Text highlights while dragging. → turned off selection everywhere but the share text
  • Caught while holding still. → still open: lifting your finger should count as frozen
  • Make the right number more obvious. → Easy and Hard modes are in mockups

A global leaderboard: Today's Crew


Sample board for illustration.

The backend is tiny: one Python Lambda behind a function URL, plus one DynamoDB table keyed by vault and device. It costs pennies.

  • Never block sharing. You always see your result first. You go on the board under three random letters, and you can tap your row any day to sign your real initials.
  • No bad words in three letters. There's a blocklist, checked in the game and on the server. Try one and you get an Easter egg: muzzle flash, gunshot, BANG., and your letters get shot out.

What's next

  • Fair freezing
  • Easy / Hard modes
  • Real art by Ally
  • The actual GraLab controller, on a screen at Wonderville

New vault every night. Come crack it: haugf.com/vault

articles.title: AI SDK 7.0.163 Added Two Stream Parts in a Patch Release. My Exhaustive Switch Stopped Compiling
articles.description: Upgrading ai from 7.0.162 to 7.0.163+ adds ping and steering-message to TextStreamPart, so an assertNever switch over fullStream stops compiling. Tested fix and runtime behavior.
articles.body_html:
If you loop over fullStream from streamText and switch on part.type with an assertNever fallback, bumping ai from 7.0.162 to anything from 7.0.163 up will break your type check. Nothing is wrong at runtime. The union just got two new members in a patch release.

I hit this on purpose to see exactly what changes, so here's the error, why it happens, and the fix.

The error

This is a normal exhaustive handler. It compiles cleanly against ai@7.0.162:

import type { TextStreamPart, ToolSet } from 'ai';

function assertNever(value: never): never {
  throw new Error(`Unhandled stream part: ${JSON.stringify(value)}`);
}

export function describePart(part: TextStreamPart<ToolSet>): string {
  switch (part.type) {
    case 'start':
    case 'start-step':
    case 'finish-step':
    case 'finish':
      return part.type;
    case 'text-start':
    case 'text-end':
    case 'reasoning-start':
    case 'reasoning-end':
      return part.type;
    case 'text-delta':
    case 'reasoning-delta':
      return part.text;
    case 'tool-input-start':
    case 'tool-input-delta':
    case 'tool-input-end':
    case 'tool-call':
    case 'tool-result':
    case 'tool-error':
    case 'tool-output-denied':
    case 'tool-approval-request':
    case 'tool-approval-response':
      return part.type;
    case 'source':
    case 'file':
    case 'reasoning-file':
    case 'custom':
    case 'raw':
      return part.type;
    case 'abort':
      return 'aborted';
    case 'error':
      return `error: ${String(part.error)}`;
    default:
      return assertNever(part);
  }
}

Same file, same tsc (TypeScript 7.0.2), with ai@7.0.165 installed:

src/handle.ts(43,26): error TS2345: Argument of type 'TextStreamPingPart | TextStreamSteeringMessagePart' is not assignable to parameter of type 'never'.
  Type 'TextStreamPingPart' is not assignable to type 'never'.

Where the two new parts come from

Both landed in ai 7.0.163 (Nov 5, 2026):

  • ping is a typed streaming heartbeat. The release note is direct about it: "Consumers with exhaustive stream-part switches must handle the new ping union variant when upgrading, even when the opt-in is disabled." According to the release note, Anthropic emits it only when you pass includePings: true (added in @ai-sdk/anthropic 4.0.97, off by default).
  • steering-message comes from the "stream steering messages to the ui" change. It shows up when a steering message gets added to a running agent loop, and it carries id, message (the user message) and stepNumber.

So even if you never turn pings on and never use steering, your switch still has to account for both. The type is the contract, not what your provider happens to send today.

The fix

Add the two cases. A ping has nothing to render, so I return null and widen the return type:

export function describePart(part: TextStreamPart<ToolSet>): string | null {
  switch (part.type) {
    case 'ping':
      return null; // keep-alive only, nothing to render
    case 'steering-message':
      return `steering: ${part.id} (step ${part.stepNumber})`;
    // ...every case from before, unchanged...
    default:
      return assertNever(part);
  }
}

That compiles clean on 7.0.165.

What a ping looks like at runtime

I wanted to know where pings actually surface, so I fed streamText a MockLanguageModelV4 (from ai/test) that emits two ping chunks around some text, then read both fullStream and toUIMessageStream(). Output on ai@7.0.165, Node 22.23.4:

fullStream: start,start-step,ping,text-start,text-delta,ping,text-delta,text-end,finish-step,finish
text: "Hello world"
uiMessageStream: start,start-step,text-start,text-delta,text-delta,text-end,finish-step,finish

That matches the release note. Pings come through fullStream, they don't end up in the generated text, and they're dropped from the UI message stream. So if your frontend only consumes useChat and the UI stream, you won't see them. The type error only bites code that walks fullStream (or the stream property) on the server.

This isn't the first time

The AI SDK changelog has flagged the same kind of break in patch releases before. 7.0.149 added interrupted to the finish-reason types and warned that exhaustive switches and Record<FinishReason, string> maps need updating. 7.0.129 did the same with a new max reasoning level. If you keep exhaustive checks (and I'd keep them, since they're how you find out about new parts at all), two habits help:

  • Pin ai to an exact version and bump it in its own commit, so a red tsc points straight at the upgrade.
  • Read the changelog for "exhaustive" before bumping. The maintainers have been good about calling these out.

The other option is dropping assertNever for a default: return null. That compiles forever, but then new parts like steering-message slip by silently, and that's arguably worse than a build error you fix in two lines.

Do you keep exhaustive switches over fullStream, or did you give up on them after the third patch-release break?

Tested Nov 9, 2026 with ai 7.0.162 and 7.0.165, @ai-sdk/anthropic 4.0.99 (type definitions only, no live Anthropic calls), TypeScript 7.0.2 and Node 22.23.4. The runtime output comes from a mock model, not a real provider stream.

articles.title: Three event sites already hand you their data. Here's where each one hides it 🗂️
articles.description: No CSS selectors, no headless browser. The data was in the HTML all along.  This week I built one...
articles.body_html:
No CSS selectors, no headless browser. The data was in the HTML all along.

This week I built one that collects upcoming events in a city from Eventbrite, Meetup and Luma and puts them in one list. I expected three scrapers full of fragile selectors. I ended up writing almost none, because all three sites already ship their event data inside the page, in a form a program can read. Each one just keeps it somewhere different.

🚦 First, the rules

Before writing any code I read each site's robots.txt, keeping only the rules that apply to every bot (User-agent: *):

  • Eventbrite blocks its RSS and Atom feeds, checkout links and a few API paths. The city search pages (/d/...) and event pages are open.
  • Meetup blocks its API paths (/api, /meetup_api) and its feeds. The search page (/find/) and event pages are open.
  • Luma's robots.txt only has rules for Googlebot.

robots.txt isn't the whole story, so read each site's terms as well before you build on it. I also send an honest User-Agent that names the tool, and wait 1.5 seconds between requests to the same site.

🧩 Hiding place 1: schema.org JSON-LD

All three sites put a <script type="application/ld+json"> block in their pages, with each event described in schema.org's Event vocabulary. It's there for search engines, and it's the most standard of the three hiding places:

{
  "@type": "Event",
  "name": "Tech Networking Event In NYC",
  "startDate": "2026-11-18",
  "location": {
    "@type": "Place",
    "name": "Tap Haus 33",
    "address": { "streetAddress": "14 East 33rd Street", "addressLocality": "New York" },
    "geo": { "latitude": "40.7473297", "longitude": "-73.9842987" }
  }
}

The events can be nested inside @graph arrays or ItemLists, and the type can be MusicEvent or BusinessEvent rather than plain Event. So instead of guessing the shape, I walk the whole object and keep anything whose type ends in "Event":

export function jsonLdEvents(html) {
    const events = [];
    const walk = (node) => {
        if (!node || typeof node !== 'object') return;
        if (Array.isArray(node)) return node.forEach(walk);
        const type = [].concat(node['@type'] ?? []).join(' ');
        if (/Event\b/.test(type)) events.push(node);
        for (const value of Object.values(node)) walk(value);
    };
    for (const m of html.matchAll(/<script[^>]*application\/ld\+json[^>]*>([\s\S]*?)<\/script>/gi)) {
        try { walk(JSON.parse(m[1])); } catch { /* one broken block shouldn't hide the rest */ }
    }
    return events;
}

JSON-LD is great for the basics. But it's the search-engine version of each event, so it leaves things out. Meetup's had no coordinates and no end time, and Eventbrite's search page had no prices. For the rest, I went to the data each site's own front end uses.

🧩 Hiding place 2: a JavaScript object (Eventbrite)

Eventbrite's search page is about 800 KB, and most of that is one line:

window.__SERVER_DATA__ = {"env":{...},"search_data":{"events":{"results":[...],"pagination":{...}}}, ...};

It isn't a JSON script tag, so you can't just grab a script's contents and parse them. It's a JavaScript assignment, followed by more code. I find the marker, then walk forward counting braces until the object closes, skipping anything inside strings. Event descriptions are full of { and }, so strings have to be skipped, escaped quotes included:

export function objectAfter(html, marker) {
    const start = html.indexOf('{', html.indexOf(marker));
    let depth = 0, inString = false, escaped = false;
    for (let i = start; i < html.length; i++) {
        const c = html[i];
        if (inString) {
            if (escaped) escaped = false;
            else if (c === '\\') escaped = true;
            else if (c === '"') inString = false;
            continue;
        }
        if (c === '"') inString = true;
        else if (c === '{') depth++;
        else if (c === '}' && --depth === 0) return JSON.parse(html.slice(start, i + 1));
    }
    return null;
}

That object holds 20 events a page, each with the venue's full address, coordinates, time zone, categories and an is_online_event flag, plus page_count for paging with ?page=2.

🧩 Hiding place 3: Next.js page data (Luma and Meetup)

Luma and Meetup are both Next.js apps, so each page carries <script id="__NEXT_DATA__"> with the props it was rendered from.

Luma is the easy one. A city page like luma.com/london has its events at props.pageProps.initialData.data.events, with the ticket price in cents, whether it's free, the guest count and the host calendar. Luma's discover page lists the cities it covers (87 when I checked), each with coordinates, so I pick the nearest one to the place the user typed.

Meetup ships an Apollo cache instead, which is normalized: objects point at each other by reference rather than nesting.

const state = nextData.props.pageProps.__APOLLO_STATE__;
// ROOT_QUERY['eventSearch:{"filter":{"city":"New York",...}}'] = { edges: [{ node: { __ref: 'Event:316963808' } }, ...] }
// state['Event:316963808'] = { title, dateTime, venue, group: { __ref: 'Group:11913282' }, rsvps: { totalCount: 147 }, ... }
const resolve = (v) => (v && v.__ref ? state[v.__ref] : v);

The cache key even records the filter Meetup actually applied, city and country included. That turned out to matter.

🐛 The bug: zero Meetup events, but only sometimes

With a keyword ("tech"), Meetup returned about 20 to 30 events per city. Without one, it returned zero for every city. No error, just nothing.

The page wasn't empty. Without a keyword, Meetup doesn't run a search at all. It shows recommended events, and those are cached under a different key with a different shape:

// with a keyword:    eventSearch:{...}       -> edges: [{ node: { __ref: 'Event:1' } }]
// without a keyword: recommendedEvents:{...} -> edges: [{ __ref: 'RecommendedEventsEdge:{"node":{"id":"1"}}' }]

Each edge is a reference too, so the event is two hops away. The fix was to accept either key and resolve twice:

const key = keys.find((k) => k.startsWith('eventSearch')) ?? keys.find((k) => k.startsWith('recommendedEvents'));
const events = state.ROOT_QUERY[key].edges.map((edge) => resolve(resolve(edge)?.node));

Lesson: when a parser returns zero, test with and without every optional input. "Empty" was a different page shape, not an empty page.

📍 Every site wants the place spelled differently

The user types "London". Each site wants something else:

Site What it wants
Eventbrite /d/united-kingdom--london/ (/d/ny--new-york/ in the US)
Meetup location=gb--London (us--ny--New York in the US and Canada)
Luma the nearest of its city slugs: london

So the first step is a geocoder (OpenStreetMap's Nominatim) for the country, the state code and coordinates. It had two surprises:

  • OpenStreetMap calls London "Greater London", and New York "City of New York". My first London run searched "Greater London" on Eventbrite and Meetup. (Luma was fine, because it goes by coordinates.) Now a prefix like that is dropped when what's left is what the user typed.
  • Meetup quietly falls back to your own location. When I sent a location string it didn't understand (location=london, or bare coordinates), it didn't fail. It returned events near my IP address, which is in Nairobi. The venues gave it away: every one of them was in or around Nairobi. Now every source checks the place it actually searched, and a mismatch becomes an error row for that city instead of wrong events.

A real mismatch needs care too. Eventbrite searches "Brooklyn" as New York, which is fair, since Brooklyn is part of the city. So the check accepts the parent city the geocoder reports.

🕐 Three time formats, one output

  • Eventbrite: "start_date": "2026-11-18", "start_time": "18:30", "timezone": "America/New_York"
  • Luma: "start_at": "2026-11-08T23:00:00.000Z" plus a time zone
  • Meetup: "dateTime": "2026-11-10T19:30:00-05:00"

I output local time with the offset (2026-11-18T18:30:00-05:00), because that's when people turn up, and it still converts cleanly. Node's Intl gives the offset for any zone at a given moment:

function offsetAt(timeZone, utcMs) {
    const name = new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-US', { timeZone, timeZoneName: 'longOffset' })
        .formatToParts(new Date(utcMs)).find((p) => p.type === 'timeZoneName').value; // "GMT-05:00"
    const m = name.match(/GMT([+-])(\d{1,2}):?(\d{2})?/);
    return m ? `${m[1]}${m[2].padStart(2, '0')}:${m[3] ?? '00'}` : '+00:00';
}

For Eventbrite's local times there's a catch: to know the offset you need the instant, and to know the instant you need the offset. I guess with the naive time, then ask again at the corrected instant, so a time near a daylight-saving change lands on the right side. The unit tests cover New York in November (-05:00) and July (-04:00), London (+00:00) and Kolkata (+05:30).

🔁 The same event on two sites

Organizers often list one event in two places. A test run in London found "Tech-Baithak London Launch Meet" on both Eventbrite and Meetup. The merge key is deliberately simple: the title's words, lowercased and stripped of punctuation, plus the local start date. The first listing is kept, the other goes into an alsoListedOn field, and any field the first listing lacks (coordinates, price) is filled from the second.

🎯 What I learned

  • Look for the data before you write selectors. JSON-LD, __NEXT_DATA__ and server data objects survive redesigns that break CSS selectors.
  • Every site hides it differently. One extractor for each kind of hiding place, plus one normalizer, beat three full scrapers.
  • Normalized caches need resolving. In Apollo's cache, even the list edges can be references.
  • Check what the site actually searched. A search that falls back to your IP location looks exactly like success.
  • Test every optional input both ways. My zero-results bug only appeared without a keyword.

articles.title: Ghost Hunt · Who Else Was There? Every face has a heartbeat. Except one.
articles.description: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge.           Signals 7 live Presage...
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge.
Signals 7 live Presage SmartSpectra signals: pulse, chest movement, breathing rate, talking, blinks, expression, validation status
Platform Electron desktop app, English and Portuguese
Privacy Camera only after consent, no frames saved, no video recorded, SDK telemetry off
Tested 19,000 tests on fake data with a known answer
Play it now Web demo in your browser, on sample numbers. The live camera reading runs in the desktop app, because the Presage SDK is native (Node.js/Electron)
Code github.com/jenniferevangelista-de/who-else-was-there (MIT)

What I Built

Most camera-vitals apps measure the pulse that is there. Ghost Hunt is a cute, spooky game that hunts for the pulse that is missing.

Plenty of people would play it for real. In a 2009 Pew Research Center survey, 18% of U.S. adults said they had seen a ghost or been in the presence of one, and 29% said they had felt in touch with someone who had already died (Pew Research Center). Ghost Hunt gives that feeling an instrument, and a rule: nothing counts unless the camera measured it.

Marina was about to go out. At the door, a feeling hit her so hard she couldn't breathe, and she stayed home. She lives alone and saw nothing, but the hallway camera was on. Three tiny ghost hunters point a new instrument at her tape, the Ghost Detector. Living faces have a heartbeat. The face that does not is the case.

Point Ask Report

What you can do in it

  • Browse 30 nights of tape on a haunted calendar, and let the detector analyze any night.
  • Analyze the tape: drag to any second, or search the hallway with a flashlight.
  • Point the detector at one spot: it finds the second face and locks on. 0 beats per minute.
  • Collect evidence cards that jump to the exact moment on the tape.
  • Ask the spirit on a board that moves only when you breathe out, and waits if you talk.
  • Learn what it is. Each spirit gets one of seven kinds, picked from the evidence: Guardian, Haunter, Watcher, Intruder, Shade, Veiled or Visitor. Luna, the medium, deciphers what it wants. Dr. Bigotes, the skeptic, refuses to sign it. Xochi writes it all down.
  • Get read yourself in The Room: your real pulse, breathing and expression, live from your camera. A figure moves only when you blink.
  • Upload your own video, once you confirm everyone in it agreed. Presage reads it as it plays, and you get a report with a verdict: is there a spirit in it?

It is a desktop app in Electron, in English and Portuguese, with original music and voices. Marina's story is drawn and tagged as sample data on every screen. The Room and uploaded videos are real SDK readings.

Demo

Demo, with the live signal:

Pitch:

Play it in your browser, no install: https://jenniferevangelista-de.github.io/who-else-was-there/ (sample numbers).

No login is needed. Without a Presage key the app opens on sample numbers, and every sample screen is tagged. With a key, The Room reads your camera live.

Code

jenniferevangelista-de / who-else-was-there

Ghost Hunt · Who Else Was There?

Every face in this video has a heartbeat. Except one.

Most camera-vitals apps measure the pulse that is there. Ghost Hunt is a cute, spooky game that hunts for the pulse that is missing. It runs on the Presage SmartSpectra SDK, which reads a person's pulse and breathing from an ordinary camera.

Entry for the DEV Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge, category Most Creative or Delightful Use.

Play it in your browser: jenniferevangelista-de.github.io/who-else-was-there (sample numbers; the live camera reading needs the desktop app)

Videos: Demo with the live signal (4:16) · Pitch (2:17)

Contents: The game in one minute · Everything you can do · The challenge's questions, answered · How the SDK is used · How we tested it · Run it yourself · Consent and data

The game in one minute

  1. A case arrives. Marina was about to go…
View on GitHub

Setup is in the README, along with a walkthrough of every screen. The SDK integration is in app/renderer/presage.js.

How It Responds to Human Signals

Seven SmartSpectra signals, and each one has a job in the game.

How to read it: each row is a signal, each column is a part of the game, and a big green dot means that signal changes something on that screen.

  • Pulse (cardio.pulseRate) drives the heart and the detector line, in real time. Readings under 50% confidence do not count.
  • Chest movement (breathing.upperTrace) moves the séance glass when you breathe out, and finds a held breath.
  • Talking (face.talking) makes the glass wait while you speak.
  • Blinks (face.blinking) are the only thing that moves the figure in the Room.
  • Breathing rate (breathing.rate) and expression (face.expression) become your numbers and your evidence cards.
  • Validation status (validationStatus) turns "multiple faces" into a second face, and poor light into "unreadable". A badly lit face is never called a ghost.

One rule keeps the spirit honest: cite or vanish. There is no language model. Every line the spirit says must cite a measured card, and every number in it must match that card, or the line is not said.

How to read it: follow the top row from left to right. The camera goes into Presage's SDK, our code turns its numbers into evidence cards, and only then can the spirit speak.

How I tested it, including where it breaks

The computer vision belongs to Presage, and I treat it as an instrument. What is mine is the logic that decides what the numbers mean, so I tested that. It works like hiding a fake ghost to see if the detector finds it: 19,000 tests on fake data where I already know the answer, reproducible with npm run benchmark. They test my rules, not Presage's accuracy, and no real person is in them.

How to read it: the left side is what I hid, the top is what the detector answered. Numbers on the green diagonal are right answers. Anything off it would be a mistake.

A living face was called a ghost 0 times in 400. Then I pushed the noise up until the rules failed, because that is the useful part.

How to read it: each number is how many of 200 tests got the right answer. Green is right, pink is wrong. Going up, the reading gets more jittery. Real jumps are always caught, but from 9 bpm of jitter the alarm starts going off by itself.

The README explains every chart and lists every limit I found.

What the SDK Taught Me

  1. Confidence is part of the signal. A pulse under 50% confidence does not count. Without that rule, a shaky reading looks exactly like a ghost.
  2. Bad light is not a spirit. The SDK's validation status says when a face cannot be read, and the game turns that into "unreadable" instead of a scary verdict.
  3. The SDK wants a real device. I tried a reading on a cloud server (GitHub Actions) and Presage refused to pair it (HTTP 403). The live readings in the demo come from a real computer with a camera.
  4. Windows can block it. With Smart App Control on, Windows blocks the SDK's unsigned libraries. The app still opens on tagged sample numbers, so nobody gets a blank screen.

Prize Categories

Most Creative or Delightful Use. The discovery here is a heartbeat that never comes, your own breath moves the glass on the board, and the blink is a jump scare with rules.

Consent and Data Handling

  • Camera consent: a rules screen comes first. The camera turns on only when you press a button, a pill at the top right turns it off at any time, and the microphone is never requested.
  • Other people's videos: the file picker stays locked until you confirm that everyone in the recording agreed.
  • Storage and retention: no frames saved and no video recorded. Readings live in memory and vanish when the app closes. A report is written only if you press Save, with numbers and words only.
  • Sharing: the app has no server of its own and sends nothing to one.
  • The SDK: frames are handed to Presage SmartSpectra inside the app, which uses your API key and Presage's authenticated channel. Presage's public documentation does not say where frames are processed, so I do not claim on-device processing. See Presage's Telemetry and Privacy page and Privacy Policy.
  • SDK telemetry: switched off (enableTelemetry: false).
  • Deletion: close the app and the readings are gone. Delete a saved report like any file.
  • AI services: none at run time.
  • Not medical: this is a game. It does not diagnose, treat or monitor anyone.

Every Requirement, Checked

The challenge asks for Where it is
A functional app on the SmartSpectra SDK app/renderer/presage.js, @smartspectra/node-sdk 3.4.0
At least one live Presage signal Seven, listed above and shown live in the demo
A DEV post on the template, with the tags This post
A public repository with setup instructions The repository above, README
A demo video Linked in Demo
Testing instructions if login is needed No login is needed
Consent, storage, sharing, retention, deletion, SDK telemetry and AI services Consent and Data Handling, above
No diagnosis or treatment claims, no medical decisions It is a game, and says so on screen
No covert monitoring Consent comes first, and other people's videos stay locked until you confirm they agreed

Built with AI coding assistance. The story, design decisions and testing direction are mine.

articles.title: Stale JavaScript in Google’s Render? Check the Asset Fingerprint
articles.description: If Google's rendered page still shows an old answer after a JavaScript deployment, check which script...
articles.body_html:
If Google's rendered page still shows an old answer after a JavaScript deployment, check which script file the public HTML references and which version the rendered output used. A changed source file in your repository does not prove the current page requests a new asset URL.

Google recommends content fingerprinting for JavaScript and CSS resources. In practice, that means a content change produces a different filename. The diagnostic task is to trace the reference, confirm the file exists, and inspect the resulting answer. Adding a random version label to a page is not enough.

This guide follows a fictional documentation update. It is a proposed debugging method, not a report that a real website or Google rendering test was run.

Understand the documented caching risk

Google's JavaScript SEO documentation says Googlebot caches aggressively and its Web Rendering Service may ignore caching headers. That can result in outdated JavaScript or CSS resources being used. Google recommends a content fingerprint in the filename so a changed resource gets a new filename.

The Web Rendering Service, often shortened to WRS, is the rendering component discussed in that guidance. Keep the claim scoped to Google's documented behavior. It does not establish how every AI crawler or browser caches scripts, and it does not prove caching caused the particular stale answer you are investigating.

Use the documented risk to form a testable hypothesis: the live HTML may still point to an asset whose URL did not change when its contents changed. Preserve competing explanations, including old HTML, an outdated data response, or a failed deployment. The next checks should narrow that list.

Follow a fictional documentation update

Imagine a public setup guide whose answer changes from “administrators only” to “administrators and editors.” In this invented example, a client-side script supplies the eligibility sentence. The team updates the script but continues publishing it at the same filename, guide.js.

A developer sees the new sentence in a freshly loaded browser. A later rendering observation still shows the old sentence. These are fictional observations illustrating the investigation. They do not establish that a fresh browser view and a Google rendering view will always differ this way.

Start by recording the URL, the deployment identifier, the exact old and new sentences, and the time of each observation. Then preserve the public HTML's script references. If the deployed page still requests guide.js, the team has a specific reference to investigate. If it requests a new fingerprinted file, follow that file rather than assuming the earlier naming mistake remains the active cause.

Inspect the public reference rather than the build folder

A local build can produce correctly fingerprinted assets while an old HTML document still references a previous release. Check the document delivered at the public URL. Record the script URLs it requests and compare them with the deployment's asset manifest or equivalent build output.

Use a small reference chain: public page, referenced script, rendered eligibility sentence. Each link in that chain answers a different question. The manifest says what the build intended to publish. The public document says what a recipient is being instructed to load. The rendered output says what content appeared in the inspected run.

Do not expose private build configuration or credentials in an SEO ticket. Usually the public asset path, deployment identifier, and a short content excerpt are enough to explain the mismatch. Keep complete diagnostic records in the team's appropriate private location when they contain internal details.

Check that the new filename represents new content

Content fingerprinting ties the filename to the file's contents. It is useful because a meaningful file change creates a different resource address. If a pipeline keeps the old filename while replacing the contents, it has not applied the approach Google describes for this problem.

In the fictional guide, a new build might reference guide.a72c.js instead of guide.19bf.js. Those names are illustrative. Confirm that the public HTML points to the intended file and that the file can be fetched through the normal public path. A new reference to a missing file creates a different failure.

Check the relevant module or generated content inside the deployed asset using approved inspection tools. Do not rely only on a filename that looks new. A configuration error can publish a new asset name with the wrong source content. The repair needs agreement between the reference and the actual answer it produces.

Deploy the document and its assets as a coherent release

A page and its dependencies need to agree during deployment. If new HTML points to files that are not available yet, readers may receive a broken page. If an old document remains available, it may continue requesting older assets. Inspect the project's established deployment behavior before proposing changes.

Keep older assets available for as long as the site's legitimate document versions can reference them, according to the project's release and retention policy. Do not delete a previous build's files simply because a new build finished. That is an engineering recommendation about dependency consistency, not a statement that Google requires one universal retention period.

When writing the issue, name the actual boundary that failed. “The public HTML still references the previous script” is more actionable than “Google ignores our updates.” It also gives the deployment owner a concrete condition to reproduce and verify without requiring access to the whole content strategy.

Compare the resulting answer under recorded conditions

After the repair, inspect the public page and record the script reference again. Then inspect the relevant rendered output using the appropriate native testing workflow. Google's documentation points to rendered HTML as the place to check what is visible after rendering. Keep the timestamp and the specific tool used with that observation.

Search for the complete eligibility sentence, including its limiting condition. Seeing the word “editors” somewhere in the page is weaker evidence than seeing the intended answer in the correct section. Also check that the sentence remains connected to its product and task so the updated passage is meaningful to a reader.

If the output remains stale, do not keep changing filenames at random. Revisit the chain. Is the document old? Is the requested file correct? Does a separate data request supply the sentence? Did rendering fail before the component finished? Record the observed break and investigate that layer. A fingerprint addresses asset identity; it cannot repair every content or rendering failure.

Close the delivery issue without overstating visibility

A useful completion note could say: “The public setup page references the current fingerprinted script, the asset loads, and the inspected rendered HTML contains the revised eligibility sentence.” Include the page URL, asset URL, deployment identifier, inspection method, and time. This is a proposed format for reporting a real check.

It does not establish that Google's stored search result has updated, that a page has gained rankings, or that an AI answer now cites it. Those outcomes need separate evidence. A live rendering inspection and a historical indexed observation may describe different moments in the page's lifecycle.

For an AI-answer follow-up, retain the exact prompt, engine, mode, date, answer, and linked sources. Check whether the updated eligibility condition survives in the response. A brand mention alone does not confirm the page was cited, and a citation alone does not confirm the condition was summarized accurately.

The practical outcome is a traceable content version. Your team should be able to explain which public document requested which asset and what answer the inspected output contained. That makes the next SEO or AI visibility question much easier to investigate with evidence.
